| (iv) | ■□■■ | □■□□ | □□■□ | ■■□■ | 3,1,**1**,**3** ✗ | 2,2,2,2 |

Only (ii) satisfies every row and column count:
- Column 1 is shaded in rows 1 and 4.
- Column 2 is shaded in rows 2 and 4.
- Column 3 is shaded in rows 1 and 3.
- Column 4 is shaded in rows 1 and 3.

**Answer: (B)**

questions.q: In Panel I of the figure below, the front view and top view of a structure are shown. Which one of the 3D structures shown in Panel II possesses the views shown in Panel I?
questions.e:
**Reconstruct the structure as a height map.** Use a $3\times3$ grid of columns: $x$ = left/middle/right, and rows front/middle/back. The bottom edge of the top view is the front.

**From the top view:**
- The front-right cell is empty.
- The left column splits into a front cell and a two-cell back strip.
- The right part has an L-shaped face (front-middle, middle-middle, middle-right) and a two-cell back strip.

Each face in the top view is a region of equal height.

**From the front view:**
- The silhouette is 3 high on the left and 2 high elsewhere.
- One L-shaped front face covers left-$z$0–2 and middle-$z$0–1, so the front-left column is 2 high and the front-middle column is 1 high.

Combining both views gives the only consistent heights:

$$\begin{array}{c|ccc} & \text{left} & \text{mid} & \text{right}\\\hline \text{back} & 3 & 2 & 2\\ \text{middle} & 3 & 1 & 1\\ \text{front} & 2 & 1 & 0\end{array}$$

Check: the front view then shows a separate face for the tall left part (set back one row), one face across the top band ($z$1–2, back row), and the small set-back cube at bottom-right. This matches Panel I exactly.

**Compare with Panel II:**
- **(i)** has a block in the front-right cell. The top view needs that cell empty. ✗
- **(ii)** has the centre cube raised to height 2. That would split the L-shaped top face and add an extra vertical edge in the front view. ✗
- **(iii)** has a part of height 3 in the middle column, so the front silhouette would be 3 high over two columns. ✗
- **(iv)** matches every cell of the height map. ✓

**Answer: (D)**

questions.q:
In the 2020 summer Olympics' Javelin throw finals, Neeraj Chopra exhibited a spectacular performance to win the gold medal. The silver medal was won by Jakub Vadlejch and the bronze medal was won by Vitezlav Vesely. There were six rounds of throws with each athlete having one throw per round. The best of all the throws of each athlete is considered for the medal. Following were the observations about the throws:

(i) The first and second rounds were dominated by Neeraj Chopra with a gold medal performance in his second throw, while the other two athletes did not have any medal winning throws in these rounds.

(ii) The throws in the last round by both Jakub Vadlejch and Vitezlav Vesely were fouls and were not considered for scoring.

(iii) After four rounds, Vitezlav Vesely was in the second position and could not improve upon his best throw in the succeeding rounds.

(iv) In the fourth round, the throw by Jakub Vadlejch was the best in that round. In which round did Vitezlav Vesely have his best throw?
questions.e:
**Where can Vesely's best (bronze-winning) throw be?**
- **(i)** In rounds 1–2, neither Jakub nor Vesely made a medal-winning throw. So Vesely's best is **not in rounds 1 or 2**.
- **(iii)** After round 4, Vesely was 2nd and never improved later. So his best is **within rounds 1–4**, which by (i) means round 3 or 4.
- **(ii)** His round-6 throw was a foul anyway, which is consistent.

**Rule out round 4.** After four rounds, Vesely (2nd) was ahead of Jakub. So Vesely's best after round 4 was greater than Jakub's best after round 4, which is at least Jakub's round-4 throw.

If Vesely's best had come in round 4, his round-4 throw would have beaten Jakub's round-4 throw. That contradicts **(iv)**, which says Jakub had the best throw of round 4.

So Vesely's best throw came in **round 3**. Jakub must then have overtaken him in round 5 (not round 6, which was a foul) to take silver.

**Answer: (A)**

questions.q: The probability that a \(k\)-digit number does NOT contain the digits 0, 5, or 9 is :
questions.e:
**Model:** treat each of the $k$ digit positions as independent and uniformly distributed over $\{0,1,\dots,9\}$.

- A single digit avoids $\{0,5,9\}$ when it is one of the other $7$ digits: probability $\tfrac{7}{10}$.
- The positions are independent, so
$$P(\text{no }0,5,9)=\left(\tfrac{7}{10}\right)^k=0.7^k.$$

**Why the other options fail:**
- $0.3^k$ is the probability that *every* digit is one of $0,5,9$.
- $0.9^k$ would correspond to excluding only one digit.
- $0.6^k$ would correspond to excluding four digits.

*Remark:* if a $k$-digit number cannot begin with $0$, the leading digit is uniform over $1$–$9$. It avoids $5$ and $9$ with probability $\tfrac79$, giving an exact value of $\tfrac79(0.7)^{k-1}$. That is not among the options, so the question intends the simpler model in which every position ranges over all $10$ digits.

**Answer: (C)**

questions.q: A cube is built using \(64\) cubic blocks of side one unit. After it is built, one cubic block is removed from every corner of the cube. The resulting surface area of the body (in square units) after the removal is __________ .
questions.e:
**Original cube.** $64 = 4^3$, so the cube is $4\times4\times4$, and its surface area is $6 \times 4^2 = 96$ square units.

**Effect of removing one corner block.** A corner unit cube has 3 faces on the outside of the big cube. Its other 3 faces touch neighbouring blocks.

- Removing it takes away its **3 exposed faces**: $-3$.
- It uncovers the **3 faces of its neighbours** that it was touching, and these are now on the surface: $+3$.

So the net change at each corner is **0**. The notch just swaps three outer unit squares for three inner ones.

The 8 corner blocks are not adjacent to one another in a $4\times4\times4$ cube, so the removals do not interact. The surface area is therefore unchanged:
$$96 + 8\times(-3+3) = 96.$$

**Answer: (D)**

questions.q:
Let, \(x_1\oplus x_2\oplus x_3\oplus x_4=0\) where \(x_1,\; x_2,\; x_3,\; x_4\) are Boolean Variables, and \(\oplus\) is the \(XOR\) operator.

Which one of the following must always be TRUE?
questions.e:
**Key idea:** $x_1\oplus x_2\oplus x_3\oplus x_4=0$ means an **even** number of the $x_i$ are 1. Since XOR is commutative and associative, this is equivalent to
$$x_1\oplus x_3 = x_2\oplus x_4 .$$

**(C):** complementing both inputs of an XOR does not change it, because
$$\bar a\oplus\bar b = (1\oplus a)\oplus(1\oplus b) = a\oplus b .$$
So $\bar x_1\oplus\bar x_3 = x_1\oplus x_3$ and $\bar x_2\oplus\bar x_4 = x_2\oplus x_4$, and these two are equal by the condition above. Always true. ✓

**Counter-examples for the others** (each satisfies the XOR condition):
- (A) $x_1=x_2=x_3=x_4=1$ gives XOR $=0$ but $x_1x_2x_3x_4=1$. ✗
- (B) $x_1=x_2=1,\ x_3=x_4=0$ gives XOR $=0$ but $x_1x_3+x_2 = 1$. ✗
- (D) all ones again gives $x_1+x_2+x_3+x_4=1$. ✗

**Answer: (C)**

questions.q:
A system has a Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) that has a reach of 1 MB . TLB reach is defined as the total amount of physical memory that can be accessed through the TLB entries. The paging system uses pages of size 4 KB . The virtual address space is 64 GB and physical address space is 1 GB . If each TLB entry stores a 4-bit process id, page number, frame number, and a 2-bit control field, then the size of the TLB (in bytes) is \(\_\_\_\_\) . (answer in integer)

Note: \(1\text{ }\mathrm{K}=2^{10},1\mathrm{M}=2^{20},1\mathrm{G}=2^{30}\)
questions.e:
$\begin{array}{ll}\text{ TLB reach } & =\text{ Number of TLB entries × Page size } \\ \text{ Number of TLB entries } & =\frac{\text{ TLB reach }}{\text{ Page size }}=\frac{1\mathrm{MB}}{4\text{ }\mathrm{KB}} \\ & =\frac{1\times 2^{20}\text{ }\mathrm{B}}{4\times 2^{10}\text{ }\mathrm{B}}=\frac{2^{20}}{2^{12}}=2^8=256 \\ \text{ Number of pages } & =\frac{\text{ Virtual address space }}{\text{ Page size }}=\frac{64\text{ }\mathrm{GB}}{4\text{ }\mathrm{KB}}\end{array}$

$\begin{array}{ll}\quad & \begin{array}{ll}\qquad & =\frac{2^6\times 2^{30}\text{ }\mathrm{B}}{2^2\times 2^{10}\text{ }\mathrm{B}}=\frac{2^{36}}{2^{12}}=2^{24} \\ \text{ Page bits } & =\log _2^{2^{24}}=24\text{ bits } \\ \text{ Number of frames } & =\frac{\text{ Physical address space }}{\text{ Frame size }}=\frac{2^{30}\text{ }\mathrm{B}}{2^{12}\text{ }\mathrm{B}}=2^{18} \\ \text{ Frames bits } & =\log _2^{2^{18}}=18\text{ bits }\end{array} \\ & \begin{array}{ll} & \text{ TLB entry bits }=\text{ Process ID }+\text{ Page number }+\text{ Frame number }+\text{ Control bit } \\ & \qquad =4+24+18+2=48\text{ bits } \\ & \begin{array}{ll}\qquad \text{ TLB size } & =\text{ TLB entry bits × bits per entry } \\ & \; =\frac{256\times 48}{8}=1536\text{ Bytes }\end{array}\end{array}\end{array}$

questions.q:
Consider contiguous allocation of physical memory to processes using variable partitioning scheme. Suppose there are 8 holes in the memory of sizes \(20\text{ }\mathrm{KB},4\text{ }\mathrm{KB}\), \(25\text{ }\mathrm{KB},18\text{ }\mathrm{KB},7\text{ }\mathrm{KB},9\text{ }\mathrm{KB},15\text{ }\mathrm{KB}\), and 12 KB . Assume that no two holes are adjacent. Two processes P1 of size 16 KB and P2 of size 9 KB arrive in that order, and they are allocated memory using the best-fit technique. After allocating space to P1 and P2, the number of holes of size less than 8 KB is \(\_\_\_\_\) . (answer in integer)

Note: \(1\text{ }\mathrm{K}=2^{10}\)
questions.e:
Step 1: Find where to allocate P1 (16 KB) using Best Fit

The best-fit method chooses the smallest hole that is large enough for the process.

We look for holes that are at least 16 KB.

The holes sizes are: 20 KB, 25 KB, 18 KB, 15 KB, 12 KB (all others are smaller than 16 KB).

The smallest one that fits is 18 KB.

So, P1 gets placed in the 18 KB hole. The leftover space in that hole is $18\text{ }\mathrm{KB}-16\text{ }\mathrm{KB}=2\text{ }\mathrm{KB}$ (this is now a new, smaller hole).

Step 2: Find where to allocate P2 (9 KB) using Best Fit

Now, P2 needs 9 KB. Again, use the best-fit method and look for holes with size at least 9 KB.

The available holes now are: 20 KB, 25 KB, 15 KB, 12 KB, and the new 2 KB hole (which is too small).

The smallest suitable hole for 9 KB is the 9 KB hole.

Allocate P2 to the 9 KB hole. After this, there is no leftover space in this hole.

Step 3: Find all holes less than 8 KB after allocation

After placing both processes, let's see the hole sizes:

- 20 KB (unchanged)

- 4 KB (unchanged)

- 25 KB (unchanged)

- 7 KB (unchanged)

- 12 KB (unchanged)

- 2 KB (created after placing P1)

(18 KB was used and became 2 KB hole; 9 KB was removed, so no leftover there)

The holes less than 8 KB are: 4 KB, 7 KB, and 2 KB.

So, there are a total of 3 holes with size less than 8 KB.

questions.q: In C runtime environment, which one of the following is stored in heap?
o: A static variable declared inside a function
An array of integers declared inside a function
A dynamically allocated array of integers created using malloc() function call
questions.e:
The correct answer is Option C.

In the C programming language, the memory of a program is typically divided into a few main parts. The two most important ones for this question are the Stack and the Heap.

  1. The Stack:

    • Think of the stack as a neat pile of books. You add a book to the top and you remove a book from the top. This is a Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) structure.

    • When a function is called, a block of memory (called a stack frame) is created on the top of the stack.

    • This stack frame stores the function's local variables, its parameters, and the return address (where to go back to after the function is finished).

    • When the function finishes, its stack frame is removed from the top of the stack. This is all handled automatically by the compiler.

  2. The Heap:

    • The heap is a large, unorganized pool of memory. It's not as neat as the stack.

    • This memory is used for dynamic memory allocation. "Dynamic" means it happens while the program is running, not at compile time.

    • You, the programmer, have to explicitly ask for memory from the heap using functions like malloc() (memory allocation) or calloc().

    • This memory stays allocated until you explicitly free it using the free() function. If you forget to free it, it leads to a "memory leak".

Now let's look at the options based on this understanding:

  • Option A: A static variable declared inside a function

    • A static variable is special. It is not stored on the stack. It is stored in a separate memory area (often called the Data Segment or BSS Segment). Its lifetime is the entire duration of the program, not just the function call. So, this is incorrect.

  • Option B: An array of integers declared inside a function

    • An array like int my_array[10]; declared inside a function is a local variable. Like all local variables, it is stored on the stack. It is created when the function starts and destroyed when the function ends. So, this is incorrect.

  • Option C: A dynamically allocated array of integers created using malloc() function call

    • The malloc() function is specifically designed to request memory from the heap. The memory you get from malloc is not managed automatically; you are in control. This is the definition of heap storage. So, this is correct.

  • Option D: Return address of a function

    • As we discussed, the return address is essential information for a function call. It is stored as part of the function's stack frame on the stack. So, this is incorrect.

Conclusion:

Only dynamically allocated memory, created using functions like malloc(), is stored on the heap. All other options refer to data stored in other memory segments like the stack or the data segment.

questions.q:
\(\text{ Consider the following three ANSI-C programs, P1, P2 and P3 }\)

Which one of the following statements is true?
o: Only P1 will compile without any error
Only P2 will compile without any error
Only P3 will compile without any error
All three programs P1, P2, and P3 will compile without any error
questions.e:
**Key idea:** A local variable (block scope, no linkage) may be declared only **once in the same scope**. Declaring the same name in an **inner** scope is legal: it simply hides (shadows) the outer one.

The three programs:
- **P1:** `int a=5;` at file scope, and `int a=7;` inside `main`.
- **P2:** `int a=5;` and `int a=7;`, both inside `main`.
- **P3:** `int a=5;` and `float a=7;`, both inside `main`.

Analysis:
- **P1 compiles.** The global `a` (file scope) and the local `a` (block scope of `main`) are in different scopes. Inside `main`, the local `a` shadows the global one, which is perfectly valid.
- **P2 fails.** Both declarations are in the same block, giving the error *redefinition of 'a'*.
- **P3 fails.** Both declarations are again in the same block, and the types also conflict: *redefinition of 'a' with a different type*.

So only P1 compiles without error.

**Answer: (A)**

questions.q:
An application executes \(6.4\times{10}^8\) number of instructions in 6.3 seconds. There are four types of instructions, the details of which are given in the table. The duration of a clock cycle in nanoseconds is _________. (rounded off to one decimal place)

Instruction
type		 Clock cycles
required per
instruction (CPI)		 Number of
Instructions
executed
Branch 2 \(2.25\times{10}^8\)
Load 5 \(1.20\times{10}^8\)
Store 4 \(1.65\times{10}^8\)
Arithmetic 3 \(1.30\times{10}^8\)
questions.e:
**Key idea:** $\text{Execution time} = (\text{total clock cycles}) \times (\text{cycle time})$, where total cycles $= \sum \text{CPI}_i \times \text{count}_i$.

**Total cycles:**
$$(2 \times 2.25 + 5 \times 1.20 + 4 \times 1.65 + 3 \times 1.30) \times 10^8$$
$$= (4.5 + 6.0 + 6.6 + 3.9) \times 10^8 = 21 \times 10^8 \text{ cycles}$$

Sanity check: the counts add up to $2.25 + 1.20 + 1.65 + 1.30 = 6.4 \times 10^8$ instructions, matching the question. The average CPI is $21/6.4 \approx 3.28$.

**Cycle time:**
$$t_{clk} = \frac{6.3 \text{ s}}{21 \times 10^8} = 0.3 \times 10^{-8} \text{ s} = 3 \times 10^{-9}\text{ s} = 3.0 \text{ ns}$$

That is, the clock runs at about 333 MHz.

**Answer: 3.0**

questions.q: Which of the following statements regarding Breadth First Search (BFS) and Depth First Search (DFS) on an undirected simple graph G is/are TRUE?
o: A DFS tree of \(G\) is a Shortest Path tree of \(G\).
Every non-tree edge of \(G\) with respect to a DFS tree is a forward/back edge.
If \((u,v)\) is a non-tree edge of \(G\) with respect to a BFS tree, then the distances from the source vertex \(s\) to \(u\) and \(v\) in the BFS tree are within \(\pm 1\) of each other.
Both BFS and DFS can be used to find the connected components of \(G\).
questions.e:
Let's examine each option one by one.

Option A: "A DFS tree of $G$ is a Shortest Path tree of $G$."

A DFS tree is constructed using Depth First Search, which explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking. This strategy does not guarantee that the paths in the DFS tree are the shortest ones from the source.

In contrast, a BFS tree (built using Breadth First Search) always yields the shortest paths (in terms of edge count) when the graph is unweighted.

Therefore, Option A is FALSE.

Option B: "Every non-tree edge of $G$ with respect to a DFS tree is a forward/back edge."

In DFS (for an undirected graph), the edges are typically classified as either tree edges or back edges. (In directed graphs there are additional classifications like forward and cross edges, but for undirected graphs only tree and back edges occur.)

Since every non-tree edge in a DFS of an undirected graph is in fact a back edge, and a back edge is included in the group denoted by “forward/back edges,” this statement is technically correct.

Thus, Option B is TRUE.

Option C: "If $(u,v)$ is a non-tree edge of $G$ with respect to a BFS tree, then the distances from the source vertex $s$ to $u$ and $v$ in the BFS tree are within $\pm 1$ of each other."

In a BFS tree, the level of each vertex corresponds to its distance (the minimum number of edges) from the source $s$.

For any edge $(u,v)$ in an undirected graph, the triangle inequality guarantees that

$|d(s,u)-d(s,v)|\le 1.$

This property holds whether the edge is part of the BFS tree or a non-tree edge.

Therefore, Option C is TRUE.

Option D: "Both BFS and DFS can be used to find the connected components of $G$."

To find connected components in an undirected graph, we can simply perform a BFS or DFS from any unvisited vertex until all vertices in that component are discovered, and then repeat for the remaining vertices.

Hence, both BFS and DFS are valid for identifying connected components.

Thus, Option D is TRUE.

In summary, Options B, C, and D are true, while Option A is false.

questions.q:
The output of a 2-input multiplexer is connected back to one of its inputs as shown in the figure.

Match the functional equivalence of this circuit to one of the following options.
questions.e:
**Key idea:** a 2 : 1 multiplexer computes $Q=\bar S\,I_0+S\,I_1$. In the figure, input 0 is the fed-back output $Q$, input 1 is the external data line (call it $D$), and $S$ is the select line:
$$Q=\bar S\,Q + S\,D$$

- **$S=1$:** $Q=D$. The output follows the input, so the circuit is *transparent*.
- **$S=0$:** $Q=Q$. The feedback loop keeps the last value, so the circuit *holds* (stores one bit).

That is exactly a **level-sensitive (gated) D latch**, with $S$ as the enable.

Why the others are wrong:
- (A) a D flip-flop captures $D$ only at a clock *edge*. Here the output tracks $D$ for the whole time $S=1$, so the circuit is level-triggered, not edge-triggered.
- (C), (D) a half-adder and a demultiplexer are combinational circuits with no feedback and no memory.

**Answer: (B)**

questions.q: A particular number is written as 132 in radix-4 representation. The same number in radix-5 representation is ____________.
questions.e:
**Key idea:** convert radix-4 to decimal by place values, then decimal to radix-5 by repeated division.

$$132_4 = 1\cdot4^2 + 3\cdot4 + 2 = 16 + 12 + 2 = 30$$

Repeated division by 5:
- $30 \div 5 = 6$, remainder $0$
- $6 \div 5 = 1$, remainder $1$
- $1 \div 5 = 0$, remainder $1$

Reading the remainders from bottom to top gives $110_5$.

**Check:** $1\cdot25 + 1\cdot5 + 0 = 30$.

**Answer: 110**

questions.q:
Consider a sequential digital circuit consisting of T flip-flops and D flip-flops as shown in the figure. CLKIN is the clock input to the circuit. At the beginning, Q1, Q2 and Q3 have values 0, 1 and 1, respectively.

Which one of the given values of (Q1, Q2, Q3) can NEVER be obtained with this digital circuit?
questions.e:
**Key idea:** write the next-state equations from the wiring and trace the state sequence from the given start. Any state not on that path can never appear.

Wiring: $T_1=\overline{Q_3}$ (through the inverter), $D_2=Q_1$, $T_3=Q_2$. A T flip-flop gives $Q^+=T\oplus Q$, so
$$Q_1^+=Q_1\oplus\overline{Q_3},\qquad Q_2^+=Q_1,\qquad Q_3^+=Q_3\oplus Q_2.$$

Tracing from $(Q_1,Q_2,Q_3)=(0,1,1)$:

| Present | $Q_1^+$ | $Q_2^+$ | $Q_3^+$ | Next |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 011 | $0\oplus0=0$ | 0 | $1\oplus1=0$ | 000 |
| 000 | $0\oplus1=1$ | 0 | $0\oplus0=0$ | 100 |
| 100 | $1\oplus1=0$ | 1 | $0\oplus0=0$ | 010 |
| 010 | $0\oplus1=1$ | 0 | $0\oplus1=1$ | 101 |
| 101 | $1\oplus0=1$ | 1 | $1\oplus0=1$ | 111 |
| 111 | $1\oplus0=1$ | 1 | $1\oplus1=0$ | 110 |
| 110 | $1\oplus1=0$ | 1 | $0\oplus1=1$ | 011 (start) |

The circuit cycles through 7 states: 011, 000, 100, 010, 101, 111, 110. The only 3-bit state missing is **001**.

(B) 100, (C) 101 and (D) 111 all appear in the cycle.

**Answer: (A)**

questions.q:
The police arrested four criminals - P, Q, R and S. The criminals knew each other. They made the following statements:

P says "Q committed the crime."

Q says "S committed the crime."

R says "I did not do it."

S says "What Q said about me is false."

Assume only one of the arrested four committed the crime and only one of the statements made above is true. Who committed the crime?
questions.e:
**Key idea:** S's statement, "What Q said about me is false", is the exact negation of Q's statement, "S committed the crime". So **exactly one of Q's and S's statements is true**, whatever the facts.

Only one statement in total is true, and it must be Q's or S's. So both remaining statements are **false**:
- R's "I did not do it" is false, so **R committed the crime**.
- P's "Q committed the crime" is false, so Q is innocent (consistent).

**Check with R as the culprit:**

| Statement | Truth |
|---|---|
| P: "Q committed the crime" | False |
| Q: "S committed the crime" | False |
| R: "I did not do it" | False |
| S: "What Q said about me is false" | True |

Exactly one statement is true, as required. If P, Q or S were the culprit instead, R's statement would be true along with one of Q's or S's, giving at least two true statements.

**Answer: (B)**

questions.q:
"A recent High Court judgement has sought to dispel the idea of begging as a disease — which leads to its stigmatization and criminalization — and to regard it as a symptom. The underlying disease is the failure of the state to protect citizens who fall through the social security net."

Which of the following statements can be inferred from the given passage?
o: Beggars are created because of the lack of social welfare schemes
Beggars are lazy people who beg because they are unwilling to work
Begging is an offence that has to be dealt with firmly
Begging has to be banned because it adversely affects the welfare of the state
questions.e:
**Key idea:** The passage uses a disease/symptom metaphor. Begging is **not** the disease, so it should not be stigmatised or criminalised; it is a **symptom**. The real disease is "the failure of the state to protect citizens who fall through the social security net." So people are driven to begging because social welfare protection fails them, which is option (A).

Why the others fail:
- **(B) Beggars are lazy**: blames the individual, which is exactly the view the judgement rejects.
- **(C) Begging is an offence to be dealt with firmly**: the judgement seeks to *dispel* the criminalisation of begging.
- **(D) Begging has to be banned**: treats the symptom as the problem. The passage places the problem in the state's welfare failure, not in begging itself.

**Answer: (A)**
questions.note: Not a real conflict: the GATE Overflow book lists "Beggars are lazy..." as A and "Beggars are created because of the lack of social welfare schemes" as B. Both keys pick the welfare-schemes option, which is option A in the stored order. The ExamSIDE letter A is correct here.

questions.q: Let \(G\) be an edge-weighted undirected graph with positive edge weights. Suppose a positive constant \(\alpha\) is added to the weight of every edge. Which ONE of the following statements is TRUE about the minimum spanning trees (MSTs) and shortest paths (SPs) in G before and after the edge weight update?
o: Every MST remains an MST, and every SP remains an SP.
MSTs need not remain MSTs, and every SP remains an SP.
Every MST remains an MST, and SPs need not remain SPs.
MSTs need not remain MSTs, and SPs need not remain SPs.
questions.e:
Let’s break down the effect of adding a constant $\alpha$ (with $\alpha >0$) to every edge weight in the graph.

Minimum Spanning Trees (MSTs):

Any spanning tree of a graph on $n$ vertices has exactly $n-1$ edges.

If a spanning tree $T$ originally has weight $w(T)$, after the update its weight becomes

$w'(T)=w(T)+(n-1)\alpha .$

Since every spanning tree gets exactly the same constant added, the ordering of the total weights remains identical. Hence, if a spanning tree was minimum before, it remains minimum after the update.

Shortest Paths (SPs):

A shortest path between two vertices is chosen among possibly many paths that can have differing numbers of edges.

For any path with $k$ edges, adding $\alpha$ to each edge increases the total weight by $k\alpha$. Therefore, the new weight is

$\text{new weight}=\text{original weight}+k\alpha .$

Two different paths between the same vertices may change order if one path uses more edges than the other. A concrete example can illustrate this:

Consider vertices A, B, and C with two paths from A to B:

Direct path: edge $AB$ with weight $100$.

Indirect path: edges $AC$ and $CB$ with weights $1$ each, so total weight $2$.

Originally, the indirect path is much shorter (cost = $2$ versus $100$).

After adding $\alpha =100$ to every edge:

Direct path: cost becomes $100+100=200$.

Indirect path: cost becomes $(1+100)+(1+100)=202$.

Now, the direct path becomes the shorter one, indicating the previous shortest path (the indirect one) is no longer the shortest.

Thus, while every MST remains an MST after the update, the shortest paths need not remain the same.

The correct answer is:

Every MST remains an MST, and SPs need not remain SPs (Option C).

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the use of backpatching in a compiler for

(I) Backpatching can be used to generate code for Boolean expression in one pass.

(II) Backpatching can be used to generate code for flow-of-control statements in one pass.

Which ONE of the following options is CORRECT?
questions.e:
Backpatching is a technique where jump addresses are left unspecified and later “patched” once the target addresses are known. This is particularly useful in a one-pass compiler for handling constructs that involve jumps, such as Boolean expressions and flow-of-control statements.

Here's how it applies to both statements:

$\text{Boolean Expressions:}$

When translating Boolean expressions (especially those with short-circuit behavior), we often create lists for true and false jump addresses.

Backpatching lets us fill in these addresses later, once the complete control flow is determined.

This allows the code for Boolean expressions to be generated in one pass.

$\text{Flow-of-Control Statements:}$

Statements like if, while, and for involve jumps to different parts of the code.

By using backpatching, the compiler can defer specifying the jump targets until it has processed the entire structure of the statement.

This, too, enables one-pass code generation for these constructs.

Since backpatching serves both purposes:

Statement (I) is correct.

Statement (II) is also correct.

Thus, the correct answer is:

Option C: Both (I) and (II) are correct.

Consider the following Boolean expression for \(F:\)
\(F(P,\; Q,\; R,\; S)=PQ+\overline{P}QR+\overline{P}Q\overline{R}S.\)
The minimal sum-of-products form of \(F\) is
questions.e:
Every term contains $Q$, so factor it out and apply $X + \bar X Y = X + Y$ repeatedly:

$$F = Q\,(P + \bar P R + \bar P\bar R S)$$

- $P + \bar P R = P + R$
- $(P + R) + \bar P\bar R S = (P + R) + \overline{(P+R)}\,S = P + R + S$

$$F = Q(P + R + S) = PQ + QR + QS$$

These three terms are the prime implicants of $F$, and each is essential (e.g. $PQ\bar R\bar S$ is covered only by $PQ$, $\bar PQR\bar S$ only by $QR$, $\bar PQ\bar RS$ only by $QS$), so this is the minimal SOP.

Consider the statement
"Not all that glitters is gold"
Predicate glitters\((x)\) is true if \(x\) glitters and
predicate gold\((x)\) is true if \(x\) is gold.

Which one of the following logical formulae represents the above statement?
questions.e:
**Key idea:** "Not all $A$ are $B$" is the negation of $\forall x\,(A(x)\rightarrow B(x))$, which turns into an existential.

"All that glitters is gold" is $\forall x\,(glitters(x)\Rightarrow gold(x))$. Negating it:
$$\neg\forall x\,(glitters(x)\Rightarrow gold(x))\equiv\exists x\,\neg(\neg glitters(x)\lor gold(x))\equiv\exists x\,(glitters(x)\land\neg gold(x)).$$
That is, something glitters but is not gold, which is option (D).

Why the others fail:
- **(A)** says nothing that glitters is gold. That is far stronger than "not all".
- **(B)** says all gold glitters. That is a different statement: the converse direction, and not negated.
- **(C)** says something gold does not glitter. It swaps the roles of the two predicates.

**Answer: (D)**

questions.q: Suppose you break a stick of unit length at a point chosen uniformaly at random. Then the expected length of the shorter stick is __________________.
questions.e:
Let the break point be $U\sim\text{Uniform}(0,1)$. The two pieces have lengths $U$ and $1-U$, so the shorter piece is
$$S = \min(U,\, 1-U).$$

The graph of $\min(u,1-u)$ is a "tent" that is symmetric about $u=1/2$, so
$$E[S] = \int_0^1 \min(u,1-u)\,du = 2\int_0^{1/2} u\,du = 2\cdot\frac{(1/2)^2}{2} = \frac14.$$

Intuition: the shorter piece's length is uniform on $[0, \tfrac12]$, so its mean is $\tfrac14$. The longer piece then has expected length $1-\tfrac14=\tfrac34$.

**Answer: 0.25**

questions.q: A relation r(A, B) in a relational database has 1200 tuples. The attribute A has integer values ranging from 6 to 20, and the attribute B has integer values ranging from 1 to 20. Assume that the attributes A and B are independently distributed. The estimated number of tuples in the output of σ(A>10)∨(B=18)(r) is ______
questions.e:
To estimate the number of tuples resulting from the selection $\sigma_{(A>10)\lor (B=18)}(r)$, we can use the concept of selectivity and the given that attributes $A$ and $B$ are independently distributed.

Step 1: Determine the selectivity of each condition individually.

Selectivity of $A>10$:

Possible values of $A$ range from 6 to 20, totaling 15 distinct values.

Values where $A>10$ are from 11 to 20, totaling 10 values.

Selectivity $P(A>10)=\frac{\text{Number of values where }A>10}{\text{Total number of }A\text{ values}}=\frac{10}{15}=\frac{2}{3}$.

Selectivity of $B=18$:

Possible values of $B$ range from 1 to 20, totaling 20 distinct values.

There's only 1 value where $B=18$.

Selectivity $P(B=18)=\frac{\text{Number of values where }B=18}{\text{Total number of }B\text{ values}}=\frac{1}{20}$.

Selectivity of $A>10$ and $B=18$ (since $A$ and $B$ are independent):

$P(A>10\text{ and }B=18)=P(A>10)\times P(B=18)=\frac{2}{3}\times\frac{1}{20}=\frac{1}{30}$.

Step 2: Compute the combined selectivity using the inclusion-exclusion principle.

$P((A>10)\lor (B=18))=P(A>10)+P(B=18)-P(A>10\text{ and }B=18)$

Plugging in the values:

$P((A>10)\lor (B=18))=\frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{20}-\frac{1}{30}$

Convert all fractions to a common denominator (60):

$P((A>10)\lor (B=18))=\frac{40}{60}+\frac{3}{60}-\frac{2}{60}=\frac{41}{60}$

Step 3: Estimate the number of tuples in the output.

$\text{Estimated number of tuples}=\text{Total tuples}\times P((A>10)\lor (B=18))=1200\times\frac{41}{60}=820$

Answer:

820

questions.q:
Consider the following C program :

#include < stdio.h>
int gate (int n) {
    int d, t, newnum, turn;
    newnum = turn = 0; t=1;
    while (n>= t) t*= 10;
    t/=10;
    while (t>0) {
        d=n/t;
        n=n%t;
        t/= 10;
        if (turn) newnum = 10*newnum + d;
        turn = (turn + 1) % 2;
    }
    return newnum;
}
int main( ) {
    printf("%d", gate(14362));
    return 0;
}

The value printed by the given C program is _________. (Answer in integer)
questions.e:
**Key idea:** The function scans the digits from most significant to least, and keeps only every second digit: the 2nd, 4th, ... from the left.

- The first loop grows $t$ to the smallest power of 10 that exceeds $n$: $t = 100000$ for $14362$.
- `t/=10` then gives $t=10000$, the place value of the leading digit.
- In the second loop, `d = n/t` is the current digit and `n = n%t` drops it.
- `turn` alternates $0,1,0,1,\dots$, and a digit is appended only when `turn` is 1.

| $t$ | $d$ | $n$ after | `turn` (before) | `newnum` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10000 | 1 | 4362 | 0 | 0 |
| 1000 | 4 | 362 | 1 | 4 |
| 100 | 3 | 62 | 0 | 4 |
| 10 | 6 | 2 | 1 | 46 |
| 1 | 2 | 0 | 0 | 46 |

Then $t$ becomes 0 and the loop ends. The function returns $46$, the 2nd and 4th digits of $1\,4\,3\,6\,2$.

**Answer: 46**

questions.q:
Consider the following context-free grammar \(G\), where \(S,A\), and \(B\) are the variables (nonterminals), \(a\) and \(b\) are the terminal symbols, \(S\) is the start variable, and the rules of \(G\) are described as:

\(\begin{array}{ll} & S\rightarrow aaB|Abb \\ & A\rightarrow a|aA \\ & B\rightarrow b|bB\end{array}\)

Which ONE of the languages \(L(G)\) is accepted by \(G\) ?
questions.e:
Let's analyze the grammar step by step.

The grammar has the following productions:

$\begin{array}{ll}S & \rightarrow aaB|Abb, \\ A & \rightarrow a|aA, \\ B & \rightarrow b|bB.\end{array}$

We'll examine each production rule for the start symbol $S$:

For $S\rightarrow aaB$:

The string always starts with exactly two $a$'s (i.e., $aa$).

The nonterminal $B$ generates at least one $b$ since:

$B\rightarrow b$ produces a single $b$,

$B\rightarrow bB$ allows further $b$'s.

Resulting strings: $aa$ followed by one or more $b$'s, i.e.,

$\{a^2b^n|n\ge 1\}.$

For $S\rightarrow Abb$:

The nonterminal $A$ generates one or more $a$'s:

$A\rightarrow a$ produces a single $a$,

$A\rightarrow aA$ allows additional $a$'s.

After generating the $a$'s, the production appends exactly two $b$'s.

Resulting strings: One or more $a$'s, ending with $bb$, i.e.,

$\{a^nb^2|n\ge 1\}.$

Now, since the grammar $G$ can derive strings from either of these two branches, the language $L(G)$ accepted by $G$ is the union of the two sets:

$L(G)=\{a^2b^n|n\ge 1\}\cup\{a^nb^2|n\ge 1\}.$

Comparing this with the provided options:

Option A: $L(G)=\{a^2b^n|n\ge 1\}\cup\{a^nb^2|n\ge 1\}$

Option B: $L(G)=\{a^nb^{2n}|n\ge 1\}\cup\{a^{2n}b^n|n\ge 1\}$

Option C: $L(G)=\{a^nb^n|n\ge 1\}$

Option D: $L(G)=\{a^{2n}b^{2n}|n\ge 1\}$

Clearly, the derived language matches Option A.

Thus, the answer is:

Option A.

questions.q: A regular language \(L\) is accepted by a non-deterministic finite automaton (NFA) with \(n\) states. Which of the following statement(s) is/are FALSE?
o: \(L\) may have an accepting NFA with \(<n\) states.
\(L\) may have an accepting DFA with \(<n\) states.
There exists a DFA with \(\le 2^n\) states that accepts \(L\).
Every DFA that accepts \(L\) has \(>2^n\) states.
questions.e:
We’re given that a regular language $L$ is accepted by an NFA with $n$ states. Let’s check each option step by step.

Option A: “$L$ may have an accepting NFA with $

An NFA with $n$ states that accepts $L$ is not necessarily minimal. In many cases, there exists another NFA recognizing $L$ using fewer than $n$ states.

Therefore, Option A is true.

Option B: “$L$ may have an accepting DFA with $

Although converting an NFA to a DFA via the subset construction may result in up to $2^n$ states, this is an upper bound. For some languages, the minimal DFA can in fact have fewer than $n$ states. For example, consider a language like $\Sigma^*$ which can be accepted by a nonminimal NFA with several states while its minimal DFA has only 1 state.

Hence, Option B is also true.

Option C: “There exists a DFA with $\le 2^n$ states that accepts $L$.”

This is a well-known result: every NFA with $n$ states can be converted into an equivalent DFA with no more than $2^n$ states by the subset (or powerset) construction.

So, Option C is true.

Option D: “Every DFA that accepts $L$ has $>2^n$ states.”

This statement contradicts Option C. Since we know a DFA can be constructed with $\le 2^n$ states, it is false to claim that every DFA for $L$ must have more than $2^n$ states.

Thus, Option D is false.

In summary, the only false statement is:

Option D.

questions.q:
Consider the following two languages over the alphabet \(\{a,b\}\) :

\(\begin{array}{ll} & L_1=\{\alpha\beta\alpha |\alpha\in\{a,b{\}}^+\text{AND }\beta\in\{a,b{\}}^+\} \\ & L_2=\{\alpha\beta\alpha |\alpha\in\{a{\}}^+\text{AND }\beta\in\{a,b{\}}^+\}\end{array}\)

Which ONE of the following statements is CORRECT?
o: \(L_1\) is a regular language but \(L_2\) is not a regular language.
\(L_1\) is not a regular language but \(L_2\) is a regular language.
Neither \(L_1\) nor \(L_2\) is a regular language.
questions.e:
To analyze the regularity of the languages $L_1$ and $L_2$, consider the following:

Language $L_1$:

Definition: $L_1=\{\alpha\beta\alpha |\alpha\in\{a,b{\}}^+\text{ and }\beta\in\{a,b{\}}^+\}$.

Analysis: This language requires a comparison between the prefix $\alpha$ and the suffix $\alpha$. Such comparisons typically cannot be performed by a finite automaton, implying that the language is not regular.

Language $L_2$:

Definition: $L_2=\{\alpha\beta\alpha |\alpha\in\{a{\}}^+\text{ and }\beta\in\{a,b{\}}^+\}$.

Analysis: Here, $\alpha$ is a string composed only of the character 'a', and the same sequence appears at both the start and end of any string in the language. Between these sequences, any string $\beta$ of characters from $\{a,b\}$ can occur. As the pattern just involves repetition of a specific character 'a' and does not require any comparison between two arbitrary patterns, a finite automaton can recognize it. Thus, $L_2$ is considered a regular language.

In summary:

$L_1$ requires recognizing patterns that standard finite automata cannot compare, rendering it non-regular.

$L_2$ involves a construct that a finite automaton can manage, making it regular.

questions.q: Suppose only one multiplexer and one inverter are allowed to be used to implement any Boolean function of \(n\) variables. What is the minimum size of the multiplexer needed?
questions.e:
**Key idea:** use $n-1$ of the variables as the MUX select lines and feed the last variable into the data inputs.

**A $2^{n-1}$-to-1 MUX is enough.**
1. Connect $x_1,\dots,x_{n-1}$ to the $n-1$ select lines.
2. For each select combination, the function reduces to a function of $x_n$ alone. Only four are possible: $0$, $1$, $x_n$ or $\bar x_n$.
3. Constants 0 and 1 are available, and the single inverter produces $\bar x_n$, which can fan out to as many data inputs as needed.

So every $n$-variable function can be built with one $2^{n-1}$-to-1 MUX and one inverter (Shannon expansion on $x_n$).

**A smaller MUX does not work in general.** A $2^{n-2}$-to-1 MUX has only $n-2$ select lines, so each data input would need an arbitrary function of the 2 remaining variables, such as $x_{n-1}\oplus x_n$. A single inverter cannot produce such functions.

$2^n$-to-1 also works but is not minimal, and $2^{n+1}$-to-1 is larger still.

**Answer: (C)**

**Key idea:** `var x` makes `x` a **call-by-reference** parameter. Each call of `f` therefore increments the caller's variable and returns the new value, which is a side effect. The two calls in `f(x)*f(x)` return **different** values. (The statement `x:x+1` is a misprint for `x:=x+1`.)

|---|---|---|

| second `f(x)` | $6\to7$ | 7 |

questions.q:
A non-pipelined instruction execution unit that operates at 1.6 GHz clock takes an average of 5 clock cycles to complete the execution of an instruction. To improve the performance, the system was pipelined with a goal of achieving an average throughput of one instruction per clock cycle. However, it could operate only at 1.2 GHz due to pipeline overheads. While executing a program in the pipelined design, \(30\%\) of instructions encountered a stall of 2 cycles due to pipeline hazards. The speed-up obtained by the pipelined design over the non-pipelined one for this program is \(\_\_\_\_\) (rounded off to two decimal places)

Note: \(1\mathrm{G}={10}^9\)
questions.e:
**Key idea:** compare the average time per instruction, $\text{CPI} \times t_{clk}$, of the two designs. Here the clock rates differ, so the CPI ratio alone is not enough.

**Non-pipelined** (1.6 GHz, so $t_{clk} = \frac{1}{1.6}$ ns $= 0.625$ ns):
$$T_{np} = 5 \times 0.625 = 3.125 \text{ ns}$$

**Pipelined** (1.2 GHz, so $t_{clk} = \frac{1}{1.2}$ ns $\approx 0.8333$ ns). The ideal CPI is 1, and 30% of instructions stall 2 cycles:
$$\text{CPI} = 1 + 0.3 \times 2 = 1.6$$
$$T_p = 1.6 \times \frac{1}{1.2} = \frac{4}{3} \approx 1.3333 \text{ ns}$$

**Speed-up:**
$$S = \frac{3.125}{4/3} = \frac{3.125 \times 3}{4} = 2.34375 \approx 2.34$$

Equivalently, $S = \dfrac{5/1.6}{1.6/1.2} = \dfrac{5 \times 1.2}{1.6 \times 1.6} = \dfrac{6}{2.56} = 2.34$.

**Answer: 2.34**

questions.q:
The EX stage of a pipelined processor performs the memory read operations for LOAD instructions, and the operations for the arithmetic and logic instructions. Let \(t_{EX}\) denote the time taken by the EX stage to perform the operation for an instruction. For each instruction type, the values of \(t_{EX}\) and \(M\) (the number of instructions of that type in a sequence of 100 instructions for a program \(P\) ), are given in the table below. The duration of the pipeline clock cycle is 1 nanosecond. Assume that the latch time for the interstage buffers in the pipeline is negligible.

Instruction \(t_{EX}\text{ in nanoseconds }\) M
LOAD 1.8 15
IMUL 1.5 10
IDIV 2.5 5
FADD 1.7 10
FSUB 1.7 5
FMUL 2.8 15
FDIV 3.2 5
All other instruction Less than 1.0 35

When program \(P\) is executed, the number of clock cycles for which the pipeline is stalled due to structural hazards in the EX stage is \(\_\_\_\_\) . (answer in integer)
questions.e:
**Key idea:** the clock is 1 ns. An instruction whose EX operation takes $t_{EX}$ ns therefore occupies the single EX unit for $\lceil t_{EX} \rceil$ cycles. For the $\lceil t_{EX}\rceil - 1$ extra cycles, the next instruction cannot enter EX. This is a structural hazard, and the pipeline stalls for those cycles.

| Instruction | $t_{EX}$ (ns) | EX cycles | Stalls each | $M$ | Total stalls |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| LOAD | 1.8 | 2 | 1 | 15 | 15 |
| IMUL | 1.5 | 2 | 1 | 10 | 10 |
| IDIV | 2.5 | 3 | 2 | 5 | 10 |
| FADD | 1.7 | 2 | 1 | 10 | 10 |
| FSUB | 1.7 | 2 | 1 | 5 | 5 |
| FMUL | 2.8 | 3 | 2 | 15 | 30 |
| FDIV | 3.2 | 4 | 3 | 5 | 15 |
| Others | $<1.0$ | 1 | 0 | 35 | 0 |

$$\text{Total stalls} = 15 + 10 + 10 + 10 + 5 + 30 + 15 = 95 \text{ cycles}$$

**Answer: 95**

questions.q: A 5-stage instruction pipeline has stage delays of \(180,250,150,170\), and 250 , respectively, in nanoseconds. The delay of an inter-stage latch is 10 nanoseconds. Assume that there are no pipeline stalls due to branches and other hazards. The time taken to process 1000 instructions in microseconds is ________ . (Rounded off to two decimal places)
questions.e:
**Key idea:** in a synchronous pipeline every stage gets the same clock. That clock must fit the slowest stage plus the inter-stage latch delay. With no stalls, $n$ instructions on a $k$-stage pipeline take $(k + n - 1)$ cycles.

**Clock cycle:**
$$t_p = \max(180, 250, 150, 170, 250) + 10 = 250 + 10 = 260 \text{ ns}$$

**Cycles for 1000 instructions:** the first instruction needs $k = 5$ cycles to finish. Each of the remaining 999 finishes one cycle later, so
$$5 + (1000 - 1) = 1004 \text{ cycles}$$

**Total time:**
$$1004 \times 260 = 261040 \text{ ns} = 261.04\ \mu\text{s}$$

**Answer: 261.04**

questions.q:
Consider a network path P—Q—R between nodes P and R via router Q. Node P sends a file of size \({10}^6\) bytes to R via this path by splitting the file into chunks of \({10}^3\) bytes each. Node P sends these chunks one after the other without any wait time between the successive chunk transmissions. Assume that the size of extra headers added to these chunks is negligible, and that the chunk size is less than the MTU.

Each of the links P—Q and Q—R has a bandwidth of \({10}^6\) bits/sec, and negligible propagation latency. Router Q immediately transmits every packet it receives from P to R, with negligible processing and queueing delays. Router Q can simultaneously receive on link P—Q and transmit on link Q—R.

Assume P starts transmitting the chunks at time \(t=0\).

Which one of the following options gives the time (in seconds, rounded off to 3 decimal places) at which R receives all the chunks of the file?
questions.e:
Let's analyze the given problem step by step to calculate the time at which the last chunk of the file is received by node R.

We are given the following information:

  • File size = ${10}^6$ bytes
  • Chunk size = ${10}^3$ bytes
  • Bandwidth of both links P—Q and Q—R = ${10}^6$ bits/sec
  • Each byte is equal to 8 bits.
  • Negligible header size, propagation latency, processing, and queueing delays.

First, let's calculate the number of chunks:

Total chunks = $\frac{{10}^6\text{ bytes}}{{10}^3\text{ bytes/chunk}}={10}^3\text{ chunks}$

Now, let's calculate the time required to send one chunk of size 1000 bytes from node P to router Q:

Size of each chunk in bits = ${10}^3\text{ bytes}\times 8\text{ bits/byte}=8\times{10}^3\text{ bits}$

Time to send one chunk over the link P—Q = $\frac{8\times{10}^3\text{ bits}}{{10}^6\text{ bits/sec}}=0.008\text{ sec/chunk}$

Since router Q can start transmitting the packet to R immediately after receiving it with no additional delay, we know that each chunk transmitted from P takes 0.008 seconds to reach Q and be sent out by Q.

We must account for the transmission time of the final chunk. The last of the 1000 chunks sent from P will finish reaching Q at:

The time to send 1000 chunks in series from P = ${10}^3\text{ chunks}\times 0.008\text{ sec/chunk}=8\text{ seconds}$

Finally, we need to add the time taken for router Q to transmit the last chunk to node R, which is the same 0.008 seconds:

Total time for the last chunk to reach R = $8\text{ sec}+0.008\text{ sec}=8.008\text{ sec}$

So, the time at which node R receives all the chunks is:

Option B: 8.008 seconds

questions.q:
Consider the entries shown below in the forwarding table of an IP router. Each entry consists of an IP prefix and the corresponding next hop router for packets whose destination IP address matches the prefix. The notation “/N” in a prefix indicates a subnet mask with the most significant N bits set to 1.

PrefixNext hop router
10.1.1.0/24R1
10.1.1.128/25R2
10.1.1.64/26R3
10.1.1.192/26R4

This router forwards 20 packets each to 5 hosts. The IP addresses of the hosts are 10.1.1.16, 10.1.1.72, 10.1.1.132, 10.1.1.191, and 10.1.1.205 . The number of packets forwarded via the next hop router R2 is _______
questions.e:
To determine how many packets are forwarded via the next hop router R2, we need to understand the prefix matching for each destination IP address and how many packets go to each IP address. Let's analyze the forwarding table and the IP addresses:

Prefix Analysis:

  1. 10.1.1.0/24

    • Range: 10.1.1.0 to 10.1.1.255
    • Next hop: R1

  2. 10.1.1.128/25

    • Range: 10.1.1.128 to 10.1.1.255
    • Next hop: R2

  3. 10.1.1.64/26

    • Range: 10.1.1.64 to 10.1.1.127
    • Next hop: R3

  4. 10.1.1.192/26

    • Range: 10.1.1.192 to 10.1.1.255
    • Next hop: R4

IP Address Analysis:

  1. 10.1.1.16

    • Matches: 10.1.1.0/24
    • Next hop: R1

  2. 10.1.1.72

    • Matches: 10.1.1.64/26
    • Next hop: R3

  3. 10.1.1.132

    • Matches: 10.1.1.128/25
    • Next hop: R2

  4. 10.1.1.191

    • Matches: 10.1.1.128/25
    • Next hop: R2

  5. 10.1.1.205

    • Matches: 10.1.1.192/26
    • Next hop: R4

Packet Count:


  • Each IP address receives 20 packets.

  • To find the number of packets forwarded via R2, we consider the IPs that match the prefix for R2 (10.1.1.128/25):

    • 10.1.1.132: 20 packets

    • 10.1.1.191: 20 packets

Thus, the total number of packets forwarded via R2 is:

20 + 20 = 40

Therefore, the number of packets forwarded via the next hop router R2 is $40$.

questions.q:
Consider sending an IP datagram of size 1420 bytes (including 20 bytes of IP header) from a sender to a receiver over a path of two links with a router between them. The first link (sender to router) has an MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit) size of 542 bytes, while the second link (router to receiver) has an MTU size of 360 bytes.

The number of fragments that would be delivered at the receiver is ______________
questions.e:
To determine the number of fragments that will be delivered to the receiver, we need to perform IP fragmentation based on the MTU sizes of the links. The IP datagram has a total size of 1420 bytes, including a 20-byte IP header, leaving us with a data payload of 1400 bytes.

The first link has an MTU of 542 bytes. Since the IP header is 20 bytes, the maximum data size that can be sent in one fragment is:

$542-20=522\text{ bytes}$

We need to calculate how many fragments are needed for the first link:

$\lceil\frac{1400}{522}\rceil =\lceil 2.68\rceil =3\text{ fragments}$

However, the payload size of 522 bytes must be a multiple of 8 (the fragment offset field is measured in units of 8 bytes). Adjusting the payload size:

$522\div 8=65.25\Rightarrow 65\times 8=520\text{ bytes}$

So, each fragment data payload on the first link would be 520 bytes. Let's outline the fragmentation process for the first link:

  1. First fragment:
  • 20 bytes of IP header

  • 520 bytes of data

  1. Second fragment:
  • 20 bytes of IP header

  • 520 bytes of data

  1. Third fragment:
  • 20 bytes of IP header

  • remaining 360 bytes of data.

These three fragments will be examined by the router. Now, let’s consider the second link with an MTU of 360 bytes. After adding the IP header (20 bytes), the maximum data payload is:

$360-20=340\text{ bytes}$

To see how the first fragment (520 bytes) will be further fragmented:

$\lceil\frac{520}{340}\rceil =\lceil 1.53\rceil =2\text{ fragments}$

  1. Fragment 1:
  • 20 bytes of IP header

  • 340 bytes of data
  1. Fragment 2:
  • 20 bytes of IP header

  • remaining 180 bytes of data

The second fragment (520 bytes) will be split in the same manner:

  1. Fragment 3:
  • 20 bytes of IP header

  • 340 bytes of data
  1. Fragment 4:
  • 20 bytes of IP header

  • remaining 180 bytes of data

Finally, the third fragment's 360 bytes of data will be sent as one fragment:

  1. Fragment 5:
  • 20 bytes of IP header

  • 340 bytes of data
  1. Fragment 6:
  • 20 bytes of IP header

  • 20 bytes of data

Summarizing, the total number of fragments delivered at the receiver is the sum of all fragments processed through the router for the second link, which is 6 fragments.

questions.q: If \(\theta\) is the angle, in degrees, between the longest diagonal of the cube and any one of the edges of the cube, then cos \(\theta\) = _______
questions.e:
**Vector method.** Take a cube of side $a$ with one corner at the origin.
- The longest (space) diagonal is $\vec d=(a,a,a)$, with length $a\sqrt3$.
- An edge from the same corner is $\vec e=(a,0,0)$, with length $a$.

$$\cos\theta=\frac{\vec d\cdot\vec e}{|\vec d|\,|\vec e|}=\frac{a^2}{a\sqrt3\cdot a}=\frac1{\sqrt3}\qquad(\theta\approx54.7^\circ).$$

Every edge is parallel to one of the coordinate axes, so the same value holds for any edge.

**Triangle method.** Take the corner $O$, the far end $A$ of an edge from $O$, and the opposite corner $G$. The segment $AG$ is a face diagonal of length $a\sqrt2$, and it is perpendicular to the edge $OA$. So triangle $OAG$ has a right angle at $A$, and
$$\cos\theta=\frac{OA}{OG}=\frac{a}{a\sqrt3}=\frac1{\sqrt3}.$$

Option (C), $\tfrac1{\sqrt2}$, is the cosine of the angle between a *face* diagonal and an edge ($45^\circ$).

**Answer: (A)**
questions.note: Keys differ only because of option order: the original paper lists (A) 1/2 (B) 1/sqrt3 (C) 1/sqrt2 (D) sqrt3/2, so the GO key B means 1/sqrt3; with the options as listed here 1/sqrt3 is (A), so the ExamSIDE key A is correct.

questions.q: Ten friends planned to share equally the cost of buying a gift for their teacher. When two of them decided not to contribute, each of the other friends had to pay Rs 150 more. The cost of the gift was Rs. ___________.
questions.e:
Let the cost of the gift be $C$.

- Planned share with $10$ friends: $\dfrac{C}{10}$.
- Actual share with $8$ friends: $\dfrac{C}{8}$.

$$\frac{C}{8}-\frac{C}{10}=150\;\Rightarrow\;\frac{5C-4C}{40}=150\;\Rightarrow\;C=6000.$$

Check: $\tfrac{6000}{10}=600$ and $\tfrac{6000}{8}=750$, which differ by $150$.

**Shortcut.** The two friends who dropped out leave $2\times\frac{C}{10}$ unpaid. The other $8$ cover it by paying $150$ each:
$$2\cdot\frac{C}{10}=8\times150=1200\;\Rightarrow\;C=6000.$$

**Answer: (C)**

questions.q: A processor X1 operating at 2 GHz has a standard 5-stage RISC instruction pipeline having a base CPI (cycles per instruction) of one without any pipeline hazards. For a given program P that has 30% branch instructions, control hazards incur 2 cycles stall for every branch. A new version of the processor X2 operating at same clock frequency has an additional branch predictor unit (BPU) that completely eliminates stalls for correctly predicted branches. There is neither any savings nor any additional stalls for wrong predictions. There are no structural hazards and data hazards for X1 and X2. If the BPU has a prediction accuracy of 80%, the speed up (rounded off to two decimal places) obtained by X2 over X1 in executing P is ____________.
questions.e:
**Key idea:** both processors run at the same clock, so the speed-up is just the ratio of their average CPIs.

- **$X_1$:** every branch stalls for 2 cycles, so $\text{CPI}_1 = 1 + 0.3\times 2 = 1.6$.
- **$X_2$:** only mispredicted branches (20%) stall, still for 2 cycles, so $\text{CPI}_2 = 1 + 0.3\times 0.2\times 2 = 1.12$.

$$\text{Speed-up} = \frac{1.6}{1.12} \approx 1.4286 \approx 1.43$$

In time per instruction, that is $1.6\times 0.5 = 0.8$ ns versus $1.12\times 0.5 = 0.56$ ns.

**Answer: 1.43 (accepted range 1.42 to 1.43)**

questions.q: Suppose we are given n keys, m hash table slots, and two simple uniform hash functions h1 and h2. Further suppose our hashing scheme uses h1 for the odd keys and h2 for the even keys. What is the expected number of keys in a slot?
questions.e:
To find the expected number of keys in a slot when using two hash functions $h_1$ and $h_2$ for odd and even keys respectively, we need to analyze how the keys are distributed among the slots.

Given:

Total number of keys: $n$

Total number of slots: $m$

Keys are divided into:

Odd keys: approximately $n/2$ keys

Even keys: approximately $n/2$ keys

Hash functions $h_1$ and $h_2$ are simple uniform hash functions, meaning each key is equally likely to hash into any of the $m$ slots independently.

Calculating the Expected Number of Keys in a Slot:

For Odd Keys:

Each odd key hashes to any slot with probability $1/m$.

Expected number of odd keys in a slot:

$E[\text{Odd keys in a slot}]=\frac{n}{2}\times\frac{1}{m}=\frac{n}{2m}$

For Even Keys:

Each even key hashes to any slot with probability $1/m$.

Expected number of even keys in a slot:

$E[\text{Even keys in a slot}]=\frac{n}{2}\times\frac{1}{m}=\frac{n}{2m}$

Total Expected Number of Keys in a Slot:

Sum the expected numbers from odd and even keys:

$E[\text{Total keys in a slot}]=\frac{n}{2m}+\frac{n}{2m}=\frac{n}{m}$

Therefore, the expected number of keys in any slot is $\frac{n}{m}$.

Answer: Option B

questions.q: A main memory unit with a capacity of \(4\) megabytes is built using \(1M\times 1\)-bit \(DRAM\) chips. Each \(DRAM\) chip has \(1K\) rows of cells with \(1K\) cells in each row. The time taken for a single refresh operation is \(100\) nanoseconds. The time required to perform one refresh operation on all the cells in the memory unit is
questions.e:
**Key idea:** DRAM is refreshed **one row at a time**. A single refresh operation restores an entire row of a chip. All chips share the same row address, so they refresh that row **in parallel**. The total time therefore depends on the number of rows per chip, not on the number of chips or cells.

**Chips used:**
$$\frac{4\text{ MB}}{1\text{M} \times 1\text{ bit}} = \frac{4 \times 2^{20} \times 8}{2^{20}} = 32 \text{ chips}$$
All 32 chips are refreshed simultaneously.

**Rows per chip:** $1\text{K} = 2^{10}$, and each row refresh takes $100$ ns.

$$\text{Time to refresh all cells} = 2^{10} \times 100 \text{ ns} = 100 \times 2^{10} \text{ ns} \approx 102.4\ \mu\text{s}$$

Why the other options fail:
- **(A) 100 ns** refreshes only one row.
- **(C) $100 \times 2^{20}$ ns** treats every *cell* as a separate refresh operation.
- **(D) $3200 \times 2^{20}$ ns** refreshes every cell of all 32 chips one after another.

**Answer: (B)**

questions.q:
A computer system has an \(L1\) cache, an \(L2\) cache, and a main memory unit connected as shown below. The block size in \(L1\) cache is \(4\) words. The block size in \(L2\) cache is \(16\) words. The memory access times are \(2\) nanoseconds, \(20\) nanoseconds and \(200\) nanoseconds for \(L1\) cache, \(L2\) cache and main memory unit respectively.

When there is a miss in \(L1\) cache and a hit in \(L2\) cache, a block is transferred from \(L2\) cache to \(L1\) cache. What is the time taken for this transfer?
questions.e:
**Key idea:** on an L1 miss that hits in L2, L2 supplies **one L1 block**, since L1 stores blocks of 4 words. The L1–L2 data bus is 4 words wide, so the whole L1 block moves in **a single bus transfer**. That transfer costs one L2 access to read the block plus one L1 access to write it.

$$\text{Number of transfers} = \frac{\text{L1 block size}}{\text{bus width}} = \frac{4 \text{ words}}{4 \text{ words}} = 1$$

$$\text{Time} = t_{L2} + t_{L1} = 20 + 2 = 22 \text{ ns}$$

Why the other options fail:
- **(A) 2 ns** counts only the L1 write.
- **(B) 20 ns** counts only the L2 read and ignores storing the block in L1.
- **(D) 88 ns** $= 4 \times 22$ ns assumes the entire 16-word L2 block is pushed into L1 in four bus transfers. L1's block size is 4 words, so only one 4-word block is needed.

The same model gives the companion result: on a miss in both levels, $4 \times (200 + 20) + 22 = 902$ ns.

**Answer: (C)**
questions.note: ExamSIDE lists (D) 88 ns, which moves a whole 16-word L2 block into L1 in four transfers; L1 needs only its own 4-word block, a single transfer over the 4-word bus costing 20 + 2 = 22 ns.

questions.q:
A computer system has an \(L1\) cache, an \(L2\) cache, and a main memory unit connected as shown below. The block size in \(L1\) cache is \(4\) words. The block size in \(L2\) cache is \(16\) words. The memory access times are \(2\) nanoseconds, \(20\) nanoseconds and \(200\) nanoseconds for \(L1\) cache, \(L2\) cache and main memory unit respectively.

When there is a miss in both \(L1\) cache and \(L2\) cache, first a block is transferred from main memory to \(L2\) cache, and then a block is transferred from \(L2\) cache to \(L1\) cache.
What is the total time taken for these transfers?
questions.e:
**Key idea:** each level receives a block of **its own** block size. Each transfer over a 4-word bus costs one read access at the source level plus one write access at the destination level.

**Step 1: main memory to L2.** The L2 block is 16 words and the bus is 4 words wide, so the transfer needs $16/4 = 4$ transfers. Each one reads memory (200 ns) and writes L2 (20 ns):
$$4 \times (200 + 20) = 880 \text{ ns}$$

**Step 2: L2 to L1.** The L1 block is 4 words, so a single transfer is enough: read L2 (20 ns), then write L1 (2 ns):
$$20 + 2 = 22 \text{ ns}$$

**Total:**
$$880 + 22 = 902 \text{ ns}$$

Why the other options fail:
- **(A) 222 ns** $= 200 + 20 + 2$ moves only 4 words from memory to L2, but L2 needs all 16 words of its block.
- **(B) 888 ns** $= 4 \times 222$ repeats the L2-to-L1 step four times.
- **(D) 968 ns** $= 880 + 4 \times 22$ pushes all 16 words into L1, although an L1 block is only 4 words.

**Answer: (C)**
questions.note: ExamSIDE lists (D) 968 ns = 880 + 4 x 22, which sends all 16 words on to L1; after the 4 x (200 + 20) = 880 ns fill of L2, only one 4-word L1 block (22 ns) is needed, giving 902 ns.

questions.q: A \(5\)-stage pipelined processor has Instruction Fetch \((IF),\) Instruction Decode \((ID),\) Operand Fetch \((OF),\) Perform Operation \((PO)\) and Write Operand \((WO)\) stages. The \(IF,ID,OF\) and \(WO\) stages take \(1\) clock cycle each for any instruction. The \(PO\) stage takes \(1\) clock cycle for \(ADD\) and \(SUB\) instructions, \(3\) clock cycles for \(MUL\) instruction, and \(6\) clock cycles for \(DIV\) instruction respectively. Operand forwarding is used in the pipeline. What is the number of clock cycles needed to execute the following sequence of instructions?
questions.e:
**Key idea:** PO is a single stage, so a long MUL or DIV blocks the instructions behind it. With operand forwarding, a dependent instruction can do PO in the cycle right after its producer's PO ends.

The instructions:
- $I_0$: $R_2 \leftarrow R_0 * R_1$
- $I_1$: $R_5 \leftarrow R_3/R_4$
- $I_2$: $R_2 \leftarrow R_5 + R_2$ (needs $I_1$ and $I_0$)
- $I_3$: $R_5 \leftarrow R_2 - R_6$ (needs $I_2$)

| Instruction | PO cycles | WO |
|---|---|---|
| $I_0$ MUL | 4–6 | 7 |
| $I_1$ DIV | 7–12 | 13 |
| $I_2$ ADD | 13 | 14 |
| $I_3$ SUB | 14 | 15 |

- $I_0$ goes IF, ID, OF in cycles 1–3, then PO for 3 cycles (4–6).
- DIV must wait until PO is free (cycle 7) and then holds it for 6 cycles (7–12).
- ADD needs $R_5$ from DIV, forwarded at the end of cycle 12, so its PO is in cycle 13.
- SUB needs $R_2$ from ADD, forwarded at the end of cycle 13, so its PO is in cycle 14 and its WO in cycle 15.

Total: 15 clock cycles.

**Answer: (B)**

questions.q: Which of the following fields is/are modified in the IP header of a packet going out of a network address translation (NAT) device from an internal network to an external network?
questions.e:
When a packet goes out of a Network Address Translation (NAT) device from an internal network (private IP address range) to an external network (public IP address range), certain fields in the IP header are modified. Let’s examine each option to determine which fields are modified:

Option A: Source IP

Yes, the Source IP address is modified. NAT changes the source IP address from the private IP address of the internal network to the public IP address of the NAT device. This allows external devices to recognize and communicate back to the source device using the public IP address.

Option B: Destination IP

No, the Destination IP address is not changed by the NAT device when a packet is going out from the internal network to the external network. The destination remains the same as originally set by the internal device.

Option C: Header Checksum

Yes, the Header Checksum is modified. The IP header checksum is a value that is recalculated every time a change is made to the IP header (such as modifying the Source IP address). Since the NAT device changes the Source IP address, it must also recalculate and modify the Header Checksum to ensure data integrity.

Option D: Total Length

No, the Total Length field is not modified by the NAT device when the packet is sent out from the internal network to the external network. The total length field includes the header and the data section, and since the size of the packet remains the same, this value does not change.

In summary, the fields that are modified in the IP header of a packet going out of a NAT device from an internal network to an external network are:

Option A: Source IP and Option C: Header Checksum.

questions.q:
Consider an enterprise network with two Ethernet segments, a web server and a firewall, connected via three routers as shown below.

What is the number of subnets inside the enterprise network?
questions.e:
The correct answer is Option C: 6. Here's why:

To determine the number of subnets, we need to analyze the network addresses and subnet masks assigned to each segment. Let's break down the network configuration:

Segment 1:

  • Network Address: 192.168.1.0
  • Subnet Mask: 255.255.255.192

Segment 2:

  • Network Address: 192.168.2.0
  • Subnet Mask: 255.255.255.192

Segment 3 (Web Server):

  • Network Address: 192.168.3.0
  • Subnet Mask: 255.255.255.192

Subnet Calculation:

The subnet mask 255.255.255.192 provides a subnet mask of $2^{32-26}=64$ addresses.

Each of the three segments uses this subnet mask. Therefore, there are 6 subnets:

  • 192.168.1.0/26
  • 192.168.1.64/26
  • 192.168.1.128/26
  • 192.168.2.0/26
  • 192.168.2.64/26
  • 192.168.3.0/26

Key Points:

  • The subnet mask determines the number of subnets within a given network address space.
  • A subnet mask with more bits set to '1' indicates a smaller subnet size and therefore more subnets.

questions.q:
Consider the following two statements.

S1 : Destination MAC address of an ARP reply is a broadcast address.

S2 : Destination MAC address of an ARP request is a broadcast address.

Which one of the following choices is correct?
o: S<sub>1</sub> is tue and S<sub>2</sub> is false.
Both S<sub>1</sub> and S<sub>2</sub> are false.
S<sub>1</sub> is false and S<sub>2</sub> is true.
Both S<sub>1</sub> and S<sub>2</sub> are true.
questions.e:
To determine which statements are correct, let's analyze each one in the context of the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) and how it uses MAC addresses.

Understanding ARP:

ARP Request:

Sent when a host needs to find the MAC address associated with an IP address on the local network.

Since the sender does not know the target's MAC address, the ARP request is broadcast to all devices on the local network.

Destination MAC Address: Broadcast address (FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF).

ARP Reply:

Sent by the host that owns the requested IP address in response to an ARP request.

The responder knows the MAC address of the requester (it was included in the ARP request).

Destination MAC Address: Unicast address of the requesting host.

Analyzing the Statements:

Statement S₁:

"Destination MAC address of an ARP reply is a broadcast address."

Analysis:

In an ARP reply, the responding device sends the reply directly to the requesting host.

The ARP reply contains the MAC address mapping and is sent using the unicast MAC address of the requester.

Therefore, the destination MAC address is not the broadcast address.

Conclusion: Statement S₁ is false.

Statement S₂:

"Destination MAC address of an ARP request is a broadcast address."

Analysis:

When a host sends an ARP request, it does not know the MAC address of the target IP address.

To reach all possible devices that might have the IP address, the request is sent to the broadcast MAC address.

Destination MAC Address: FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF (broadcast address).

Conclusion: Statement S₂ is true.

Final Answer:

Statement S₁ is false.

Statement S₂ is true.

Answer: Option C

S₁ is false and S₂ is true.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the functionality of an IP based router.

I. A router does not modify the IP packets during forwarding.
II. It is not necessary for a router to implement any routing protocol.
III. A router should reassemble IP fragments if the MTU of the outgoing link is larger than the size of the incoming IP packet.

Which of the above statements is/are TRUE?
questions.e:
Statement I:

"A router does not modify the IP packets during forwarding."

Analysis:

IP Packet Modification by Routers:

When a router forwards an IP packet, it decrements the Time To Live (TTL) field by 1. The TTL field is used to prevent packets from looping indefinitely in the network.

Due to the change in the TTL field, the router must recalculate the IP header checksum to maintain packet integrity.

These modifications are essential for proper network operation and are part of the IP protocol specifications.

Conclusion:

Since routers modify the TTL and checksum fields during forwarding, Statement I is FALSE.

Statement II:

"It is not necessary for a router to implement any routing protocol."

Analysis:

Routing Protocols:

Routing protocols (like RIP, OSPF, or BGP) enable routers to dynamically learn network routes from other routers.

However, it is possible for a router to operate without implementing any routing protocol by using static routing.

Static Routing:

Network administrators manually configure routing tables with fixed paths.

Suitable for small or simple networks where routes do not change frequently.

In some cases, routers may rely on default routes or be configured with static entries to handle packet forwarding without dynamic routing protocols.

Conclusion:

A router can function without implementing a routing protocol by using static routing.

Statement II is TRUE.

Statement III:

"A router should reassemble IP fragments if the MTU of the outgoing link is larger than the size of the incoming IP packet."

Analysis:

IP Fragmentation and Reassembly:

Fragmentation occurs when an IP packet is larger than the Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) of a network segment.

Reassembly of IP fragments is performed only at the destination host, not by intermediate routers.

Router Behavior:

Routers do not reassemble fragmented packets during transit.

If the outgoing link's MTU is larger than the incoming packet size (including fragments), the router forwards the fragments as they are.

Reassembly by Routers:

Reassembling fragments at each router would be inefficient and is not part of standard IP routing behavior.

Conclusion:

Since routers do not reassemble IP fragments, Statement III is FALSE.

Final Answer:

Statement I: FALSE

Statement II: TRUE

Statement III: FALSE

Answer: Option B

II only

questions.q: The preorder traversal sequence of a binary search tree is 30, 20, 10, 15, 25, 23, 39, 35, 42. Which one of the following is the postorder traversal sequence of the same tree?
questions.e:
**Key idea:** in a BST preorder, the first element is the root. The following elements smaller than the root form the left subtree (also in preorder), and the larger ones form the right subtree. Apply this recursively.

Preorder: 30, 20, 10, 15, 25, 23, 39, 35, 42

- Root **30**. Left part: 20, 10, 15, 25, 23. Right part: 39, 35, 42.
- Left subtree root **20**. Its left part is 10, 15, so 10 has 15 as its right child. Its right part is 25, 23, so 25 has 23 as its left child.
- Right subtree root **39**, with left child 35 and right child 42.

```
            30
          /    \
        20      39
       /  \    /  \
     10    25 35   42
       \   /
       15 23
```

Postorder (left, right, root):

- Subtree of 10 → 15, 10
- Subtree of 25 → 23, 25
- Subtree of 20 → 15, 10, 23, 25, 20
- Subtree of 39 → 35, 42, 39
- Whole tree → **15, 10, 23, 25, 20, 35, 42, 39, 30**

This matches (D). Option (A) prints 10 before its right child 15 and 20 before 25. Option (B) prints 25 before its child 23. Option (C) prints 20 before its child 10.

**Answer: (D)**

o: q = NULL; p->next = head; head = p;
q->next = NULL; head = p; p->next = head;
head = p; p->next = q; q->next = NULL;
q->next = NULL; p->next = head; head = p;
questions.e:
**State after the loop:** `p` is the last node and `q` is the second-last node. The list has at least 2 nodes, so `q` is not NULL. To move the last node to the front:

1. `q->next = NULL;` makes the second-last node the new tail.
2. `p->next = head;` links the old last node in front of the old head.
3. `head = p;` makes it the new head.

That is option **(D)**. For example, 1→2→3→4 becomes 4→1→2→3.

Why the others fail:

- **(A)** `q = NULL` only changes a local variable. The second-last node still points to `p`, and with `p->next = head` the list becomes a cycle.
- **(B)** sets `head = p` *before* `p->next = head`, so `p->next = p`. That is a self-loop, and the rest of the list is lost.
- **(C)** produces `p → q → NULL`. Every node before `q` is lost.

**Answer: (D)**

questions.q: A transparent square sheet shown above is folded along the dotted line. The folded sheet will look like ________.
questions.e:
**Idea:** Folding a *transparent* sheet along the vertical line reflects the left half onto the right half. Both halves' markings stay visible: the right half's markings are unchanged, and the left half's markings appear as a **mirror image about the fold line**.

**Reflecting the left half:**
- The left curve rises gently from the left edge and then steeply up to the top point on the fold line. Its reflection starts at the same top point, **drops steeply**, then flattens out and reaches the right edge at about the same height as the right-hand curve.
- The right-hand curve leaves the same top point gently and then falls steeply to that same corner region.
- Together the two curves form a **lens (leaf) shape** from the fold point down to the right edge. The reflected curve is the lower boundary.
- Reflection in a vertical line keeps vertical segments vertical. So the two short **vertical ticks** still stand **upward from the reflected (lower) curve**, inside the lens.
- The right half's two **horizontal ticks** still extend **leftwards from the upper curve**, also inside the lens.

So inside the lens there are vertical marks rising from the lower arc and horizontal marks reaching the upper arc. Drawn together, they form two Γ-shaped steps. That is option (A).

**Why the others fail:**
- **(B):** The mirrored curve is drawn rising away from the fold line. The left curve is highest at the fold line, so its mirror image must fall towards the right edge. In (B) the two curves spread apart instead of closing into a lens.
- **(C):** Only horizontal lines are shown. The vertical ticks are missing.
- **(D):** The marks are attached to the wrong arcs (horizontal parts on the lower arc, the other parts on the upper arc).

**Answer: (A)**
questions.note: Apparent conflict only, caused by option reordering. This item's option A (lens with two Γ-shaped marks) is option B in the original paper, which is what GATE Overflow's B refers to. ExamSIDE's A is right for this item's order.

questions.q: There are multiple routes to reach from node 1 to node 2, as shown in the network. The cost of travel on an edge between two nodes is given in rupees. Nodes ‘a’, ‘b’, ‘c’, ‘d’, ‘e’, and ‘f’ are toll booths. The toll price at toll booths marked ‘a’ and ‘e’ is Rs.200, and is Rs.100 for the other toll booths. Which is the cheapest route from node 1 to node 2?
questions.e:
**Idea:** The total cost of a route is the sum of its edge costs plus the toll at every booth it passes through. Tolls are a = e = Rs 200, and b = c = d = f = Rs 100.

Edge costs from the figure: $1\to a = 200$, $1\to b = 300$, $1\to f = 100$, $a\to c = 100$, $a\to 2 = 200$, $c\to 2 = 100$, $b\to 2 = 200$, $b\to d = 0$, $d\to e = 100$, $f\to b = 0$, $f\to e = 100$, $e\to 2 = 200$.

| Route | Edge cost | Tolls | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1-f-e-2 | 100+100+200 = 400 | f 100 + e 200 = 300 | **700** |
| 1-a-c-2 | 200+100+100 = 400 | a 200 + c 100 = 300 | **700** |
| 1-b-2 | 300+200 = 500 | b 100 | **600** |
| 1-f-b-2 | 100+0+200 = 300 | f 100 + b 100 = 200 | **500** |

Going through f first and taking the free $f \to b$ edge avoids the expensive $1\to b$ edge (300) and the Rs 200 tolls at a and e. That makes **1-f-b-2** the cheapest route, at Rs 500.

**Answer: (D)**
questions.note: Apparent conflict only, caused by option reordering. Both keys mean route 1-f-b-2 (Rs 500). In this item's option order that route is D, so ExamSIDE's D is right here. GATE Overflow's B refers to the original paper's order (A 1-a-c-2, B 1-f-b-2, C 1-b-2, D 1-f-e-2).

questions.q:
What is the missing number in the following sequence?  
\[2,\; 12,\; 60,\; 240,\; 720,\; 1440,\; \_\_\_,\; 0\]
questions.e:
**Pattern:** Look at the ratio between consecutive terms.

$$\frac{12}{2}=6,\quad \frac{60}{12}=5,\quad \frac{240}{60}=4,\quad \frac{720}{240}=3,\quad \frac{1440}{720}=2$$

The multiplier goes down by 1 at each step: $\times6, \times5, \times4, \times3, \times2$. The next two multipliers are therefore $\times1$ and then $\times0$:

$$1440 \times 1 = 1440, \qquad 1440 \times 0 = 0.$$

The given last term, 0, matches the $\times 0$ step, which confirms the pattern.

Equivalently, the $k$-th term is $2 \times 6 \times 5 \times \cdots \times (7-k+1)$, a falling product that ends with a factor of 0.

The other options do not fit:
- 2880 would need $\times 2$ again.
- 720 would need $\times \tfrac12$.
- 0 would be a $\times 0$ step one place too early.

**Answer: (B)**

questions.q: Rahul, Murali, Srinivas and Arul are seated around a square table. Rahul is sitting to the left of Murali. Srinivas is sitting to the right of Arul. Which of the following pairs are seated opposite each other?
questions.e:
**Idea:** Four people sit at a square table, one per side, all facing the centre. Seen from above, a person's left-hand neighbour is the next person **clockwise** and the right-hand neighbour is the next person anticlockwise. Each person has exactly one left neighbour, one right neighbour and one person opposite.

**Arrangement:**
- "Rahul is to the left of Murali": going clockwise, Rahul comes right after Murali, so the order is Murali, Rahul, ?, ?.
- "Srinivas is to the right of Arul": Arul is Srinivas's left neighbour, so going clockwise, Arul comes right after Srinivas.

Two seats remain for Srinivas and Arul:
- Clockwise order M, R, S, A: Arul comes right after Srinivas. ✓
- Clockwise order M, R, A, S: Murali comes after Srinivas, not Arul. ✗

So the clockwise order is **Murali, Rahul, Srinivas, Arul**.

**Opposite pairs:** In a 4-seat cycle, seats 1 and 3 face each other, and so do seats 2 and 4. That gives Murali–Srinivas and Rahul–Arul.

If everyone faced outwards, the arrangement would just be mirrored, which does not change who sits opposite whom. So the answer does not depend on that assumption.

- (A) Rahul and Murali, and (B) Srinivas and Arul, are adjacent pairs by the given conditions.
- (D) Srinivas and Rahul are adjacent in the order above.

**Answer: (C)**
