questions.q: State the halting problem of the Turing machine.

a.text: Given an arbitrary TM M and an input w, decide whether M halts on w; this problem is undecidable (only semi-decidable).

questions.e:
**Statement.** The halting problem asks the following. Given (an encoding of) an arbitrary Turing machine $M$ and an arbitrary input string $w$, does $M$ halt on $w$?

As a language:
$$\mathrm{HALT}_{TM} = \{\langle M, w\rangle \mid M \text{ is a TM and } M \text{ halts on input } w\}.$$
The question is whether some single algorithm (a TM that halts on every input) can answer this correctly for every pair $\langle M, w\rangle$.

**Status: undecidable** (Turing, 1936). No such algorithm exists.
- The problem is *partially decidable*, i.e. recursively enumerable. A universal TM simulates $M$ on $w$ and answers "yes" if the simulation halts.
- That simulator never answers "no" when $M$ runs forever.
- The complement, "does $M$ loop forever on $w$?", is not even recursively enumerable.

**Proof sketch (diagonalization).**
1. Suppose some TM $H$ decides $\mathrm{HALT}_{TM}$.
2. Build a TM $D$. On input $\langle M\rangle$, $D$ runs $H$ on $\langle M, \langle M\rangle\rangle$. If $H$ says "halts", $D$ loops forever; if $H$ says "loops", $D$ halts.
3. Run $D$ on $\langle D\rangle$:
   - if $D$ halts on $\langle D\rangle$, then $H$ said "loops", a contradiction;
   - if $D$ loops on $\langle D\rangle$, then $H$ said "halts", again a contradiction.

So $H$ cannot exist.

**Answer: Given an arbitrary TM $M$ and input $w$, decide whether $M$ halts on $w$. This problem is undecidable (only semi-decidable).**

questions.q:
Let $L$ be a language over $\Sigma$ i.e., $L \subseteq \Sigma^*$. Suppose $L$ satisfies the two conditions given below.

i. $L$ is in NP and

ii. For every $n$, there is exactly one string of length $n$ that belongs to $L$.

Let $L^c$ be the complement of $L$ over $\Sigma^*$. Show that $L^c$ is also in NP.

a.text: L^c is in NP: for input x, guess the unique string y ≠ x of length |x| in L together with its NP certificate, and verify both in polynomial time.

questions.e:
**Key idea.** Condition (ii) turns a "no" answer for $L$ into a "yes" answer that can be checked.
- If $x \notin L$, then some *other* string $y$ of the same length belongs to $L$.
- Because $L \in \text{NP}$, the fact that $y \in L$ has a short certificate.

**Setup.** Since $L \in \text{NP}$, there is a polynomial $p$ and a polynomial-time verifier $V$ such that
$$y \in L \iff \exists c \text{ with } |c| \le p(|y|) \text{ and } V(y, c) = \text{accept}.$$

**Verifier for $L^c$.** Take an input $x$ with $|x| = n$. The certificate is a pair $(y, c)$. Accept iff
1. $|y| = n$ and $y \ne x$, and
2. $V(y, c)$ accepts, which shows that $y \in L$.

The certificate has length $n + p(n)$, which is polynomial, and every check runs in polynomial time. Equivalently, a non-deterministic TM guesses $y$ and $c$ and then performs these checks.

**Correctness.**
- *If $x \in L^c$:* by (ii), $L$ contains exactly one string $y$ of length $n$. Since $x \notin L$, $y \ne x$. As $y \in L$, a valid certificate $c$ exists, so the pair $(y, c)$ is accepted.
- *If $x \in L$:* by (ii), $x$ is the only string of length $n$ in $L$. So every $y$ with $|y| = n$ and $y \ne x$ lies outside $L$. No $c$ makes $V(y, c)$ accept, so every certificate is rejected.

This also covers $n = 0$: the empty string must then be the unique member of length $0$, and nothing is accepted.

So $x \in L^c$ iff some polynomial-size certificate passes a polynomial-time check. Hence $L^c \in \text{NP}$, which means $L \in \text{NP} \cap \text{co-NP}$.

**Answer: $L^c \in$ NP, by guessing and verifying the unique other string of length $|x|$ that lies in $L$.**

questions.q:
Suppose we have a function HALTS which when applied to any arbitrary function $f$ and its arguments will say TRUE if function $f$ terminates for those arguments and FALSE otherwise. Example: Given the following function definition.

```
FACTORIAL (N) = IF (N=0) THEN 1 ELSE N*FACTORIAL (N-1)
```

Then HALTS (FACTORIAL, 4) = TRUE and HALTS (FACTORIAL, -5) = FALSE

Let us define the function `FUNNY (f) = IF HALTS (f) THEN not (f) ELSE TRUE`

(a) Show that FUNNY terminates for all functions $f$.

(b) use (a) to prove (by contradiction) that it is not possible to have a function like HALTS which for arbitrary functions and inputs says whether it will terminate on that input or not.

a.text: (a) HALTS always returns and f(f) is evaluated only when it is known to halt, so FUNNY is total; (b) then FUNNY(FUNNY) = not FUNNY(FUNNY), a contradiction, so HALTS cannot exist.

questions.e:
**How to read the definition.**
- `HALTS(f)` means `HALTS(f, f)`: does $f$ terminate when it is given itself as its argument?
- `not(f)` means `not(f(f))`.

So
$$\text{FUNNY}(f) = \begin{cases} \neg\, f(f) & \text{if } f(f) \text{ terminates},\\ \text{TRUE} & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$

**(a) FUNNY terminates for every $f$.** Assume HALTS exists. By hypothesis it always returns TRUE or FALSE in finite time. There are two cases.
- If HALTS$(f, f)$ = FALSE, FUNNY returns TRUE at once.
- If HALTS$(f, f)$ = TRUE, then $f(f)$ terminates with some value $v$. FUNNY computes $f(f)$, which takes finitely many steps, and returns $\neg v$.

In both cases FUNNY$(f)$ terminates, so FUNNY is a total function.

**(b) HALTS cannot exist.** FUNNY is itself a function, so we may apply it to itself.
1. By (a), FUNNY(FUNNY) terminates. Hence HALTS(FUNNY, FUNNY) = TRUE.
2. So the THEN branch of FUNNY's definition is taken:
$$\text{FUNNY(FUNNY)} = \neg\, \text{FUNNY(FUNNY)}.$$
3. Let $v$ be the value of FUNNY(FUNNY), which exists by (a). Then $v = \neg v$, and no truth value satisfies this.

Seen operationally, evaluating FUNNY(FUNNY) would call FUNNY(FUNNY) again and recurse forever, which contradicts (a).

The only assumption used was that a total, always-correct HALTS exists, so that assumption is false. No algorithm can decide, for arbitrary functions and inputs, whether the function terminates. This is the undecidability of the halting problem, proved by diagonalization.

**Answer: (a) FUNNY is total, because HALTS always returns and $f(f)$ is evaluated only when it halts. (b) Then FUNNY(FUNNY) $= \neg$FUNNY(FUNNY), a contradiction, so HALTS cannot exist.**

questions.q:
Let a decision problem $X$ be defined as follows:

$X$: Given a Turing machine $M$ over $\Sigma$ and any word $w \in \Sigma$, does $M$ loop forever on $w$?

You may assume that the halting problem of Turing machine is undecidable but partially decidable.

(a) Show that $X$ is undecidable

(b) Show that $X$ is not even partially decidable

a.text: X is the complement of the halting problem: (a) a decider for X would decide HALT; (b) if X were partially decidable, HALT and its complement would both be RE, making HALT decidable.

questions.e:
**Key observation.** For every instance $\langle M, w\rangle$, "$M$ loops forever on $w$" means exactly "$M$ does not halt on $w$". So
$$X = \overline{\mathrm{HALT}},$$
the complement of the halting problem. Checking whether an input is a well-formed encoding is decidable, so ill-formed inputs do not affect the argument.

**(a) $X$ is undecidable.**
1. Suppose a TM $D_X$ decides $X$, i.e. it halts on every input with the correct yes/no answer.
2. Build $D_H$: on input $\langle M, w\rangle$, run $D_X$ and output the opposite answer.
3. $D_H$ always halts. It says "yes" exactly when $M$ does not loop forever on $w$, that is, when $M$ halts on $w$.
4. So $D_H$ decides HALT, contradicting the undecidability of HALT.

Hence $X$ is undecidable. In short, decidable problems are closed under complement.

**(b) $X$ is not even partially decidable.**
1. Suppose $X$ were partially decidable, with a TM $P_X$ that halts with "yes" exactly on the instances of $X$.
2. HALT is partially decidable by assumption, through a TM $P_H$ that simulates $M$ on $w$ and says "yes" if the simulation halts.
3. Decide HALT as follows. On $\langle M, w\rangle$, run $P_H$ and $P_X$ alternately, one step each (dovetailing).
   - Every instance belongs to exactly one of HALT and $X$, so exactly one of the two machines eventually says "yes", after finitely many steps.
   - If $P_H$ says "yes", answer "halts". If $P_X$ says "yes", answer "loops".
4. This procedure always halts and is always correct, so HALT would be decidable, a contradiction.

Hence $X$ is not partially decidable (not recursively enumerable). The general fact used here: if a language and its complement are both RE, the language is recursive.

**Answer: $X = \overline{\text{HALT}}$, so (a) it is undecidable, and (b) it is not even partially decidable, since otherwise HALT would be decidable.**

questions.q:
The aim of the following question is to prove that the language $\{M \mid M \text{ is the code of the Turing Machine which, irrespective of the input, halts and outputs a } 1\}$, is undecidable. This is to be done by reducing from the language $\{M', x \mid M' \text{ halts on } x\}$, which is known to be undecidable. In parts (a) and (b) describe the $2$ main steps in the construction of $M$. In part (c) describe the key property which relates the behaviour of $M$ on its input $w$ to the behaviour of $M'$ on $x$.

(a) On input $w$, what is the first step that $M$ must make?

(b) On input $w$, based on the outcome of the first step, what is the second step $M$ must make?

(c) What key property relates the behaviour of $M$ on $w$ to the behaviour of $M'$ on $x$?

a.text: (a) Ignore/erase w and simulate M' on x; (b) if that simulation halts, write 1 and halt; (c) for every w, M halts with output 1 iff M' halts on x, so M is in the language iff M' halts on x.

questions.e:
**Setting up the reduction.** Let
$$L = \{\langle M\rangle \mid M \text{ halts and outputs } 1 \text{ on every input}\}.$$
From an instance $\langle M', x\rangle$ of the halting problem, we build, by an algorithm, a machine $M = M_{M',x}$ with $M'$ and $x$ hard-coded into it.

**(a) First step.** On input $w$, $M$ erases $w$ (it ignores its own input), writes $x$ on the tape, and simulates $M'$ on $x$.

**(b) Second step.**
- If the simulation of $M'$ on $x$ halts, $M$ erases the tape, writes $1$ and halts.
- If $M'$ never halts on $x$, the simulation runs forever. $M$ then never reaches this step and never halts.

**(c) Key property.** The behaviour of $M$ does not depend on $w$:
$$\forall w:\quad M \text{ halts on } w \text{ with output } 1 \iff M' \text{ halts on } x.$$
- If $M'$ halts on $x$, then $M$ halts and outputs 1 on every input.
- Otherwise $M$ halts on no input at all.

Therefore $\langle M\rangle \in L \iff \langle M', x\rangle \in \mathrm{HALT}$.

**Conclusion.** The map $\langle M', x\rangle \mapsto \langle M\rangle$ is computable, since it only writes out the code of $M$. Suppose $L$ had a decider $D$. Running $D$ on $\langle M\rangle$ would then decide whether $M'$ halts on $x$, which is impossible. Hence $L$ is undecidable.

**Answer: (a) Ignore $w$ and simulate $M'$ on $x$. (b) If the simulation halts, output 1 and halt. (c) $M$ halts with output 1 on every $w$ (equivalently, on any $w$) iff $M'$ halts on $x$.**

questions.q:
Consider two languages $L_1$ and $L_2$ each on the alphabet $\Sigma$. Let $f: \Sigma^* \rightarrow \Sigma^*$ be a polynomial time computable bijection such that $(\forall x)[x \in L_1 \text{ iff } f(x) \in L_2]$. Further, let $f^{-1}$ be also polynomial time computable.

Which of the following **CANNOT** be true?
o: $L_1$ is recursively enumerable and $L_2$ is recursive
questions.e:
**Key idea:** $f$ is a computable many-one reduction from $L_1$ to $L_2$. Because $f$ is a bijection, $y \in L_2 \iff f^{-1}(y) \in L_1$, so $f^{-1}$ is a reduction from $L_2$ to $L_1$. The two languages are therefore equally hard, and every "easier than" argument works in both directions.

**(C) cannot be true.** Suppose $L_2$ is decidable. To decide $L_1$ on input $x$, compute $f(x)$ (which halts) and run the decider for $L_2$ on it. This answers "$x \in L_1$?" correctly, so $L_1$ is decidable too. Hence $L_1$ cannot be undecidable while $L_2$ is decidable.

The other three options are all possible:
- **(A)** If $L_2$ is finite, then $L_1 = f^{-1}(L_2)$ is finite and therefore in P. For example, take $L_1 = L_2 = \varnothing$ with $f$ the identity.
- **(B)** If $L_2 \in P$, then $L_1 \in P \subseteq NP$, because $f$ runs in polynomial time. This is consistent.
- **(D)** If $L_2$ is recursive, then $L_1$ is recursive and hence also recursively enumerable. This is consistent.

**Answer: (C)**

questions.q: Which of the following problems is undecidable?
questions.e:
**(A) Decidable.** To test whether $w \in L(G)$ for a CFG $G$, convert $G$ to Chomsky normal form and run the CYK algorithm, which takes $O(|w|^3)$ time.

**(B) Undecidable.** No algorithm can decide whether an arbitrary CFG is ambiguous. The standard proof reduces Post's Correspondence Problem to it: a PCP instance has a solution iff a grammar built from it is ambiguous.

**(C) Decidable.** Remove useless states from the FSA. $L(A)$ is infinite iff there is a cycle on some path from the start state to a final state. Equivalently, it is infinite iff $A$ accepts some string whose length is between $n$ and $2n-1$, where $n$ is the number of states.

**(D) Decidable.** $L(A_1) = L(A_2)$ iff the symmetric difference $(L_1 \cap \overline{L_2}) \cup (\overline{L_1} \cap L_2)$ is empty. This can be checked with product automata and an emptiness test. Alternatively, minimise both DFAs and check whether they are isomorphic.

**Answer: (B)**

questions.q: Let $A$ and $B$ be finite alphabets and let $\#$ be a symbol outside both $A$ and $B$. Let $f$ be a total function from $A^*$ to $B^*$. We say $f$ is *computable* if there exists a Turing machine $M$ which given an input $x \in A^*$, always halts with $f(x)$ on its tape. Let $L_f$ denote the language $\{x \# f(x) \mid x \in A^*\}$. Which of the following statements is true:
o: $f$ is computable if and only if $L_f$ is recursive.
$f$ is computable if and only if $L_f$ is recursively enumerable.
If $f$ is computable then $L_f$ is recursive, but not conversely.
If $f$ is computable then $L_f$ is recursively enumerable, but not conversely.
questions.e:
**$f$ computable $\Rightarrow$ $L_f$ recursive.** Run the following on input $u$:
1. If $u$ is not of the form $x\#z$ with $x \in A^*$ and $z \in B^*$, reject. Since $\# \notin A \cup B$, this split is unique.
2. Otherwise compute $f(x)$, which halts, and accept iff $z = f(x)$.

This procedure always halts, so $L_f$ is recursive.

**$L_f$ recursive $\Rightarrow$ $f$ computable.** On input $x$:
1. List $z_1, z_2, \ldots$, all strings of $B^*$ in length-lexicographic order.
2. Use the decider to test whether $x\#z_i \in L_f$ for each $z_i$ in turn.
3. Because $f$ is total, $x\#f(x) \in L_f$. So the search stops at $z = f(x)$, the only $z$ with $x\#z \in L_f$. Output it.

This always halts with $f(x)$, so $f$ is computable. Statement (A) therefore holds.

Options (C) and (D) both claim "not conversely". The converse has just been shown to hold, so both are false.

**About (B).** The same idea also works when $L_f$ is only recursively enumerable.
- Dovetail the semi-decider over all pairs (candidate $z_i$, number of steps).
- Because $f$ is total, $x\#f(x)$ is eventually accepted, and no other $z$ can ever be accepted.

So $f$ is computable iff $L_f$ is RE as well, which makes statement (B) also mathematically true. The question thus has two true statements; the intended answer is (A).

**Answer: (A)**
questions.note: Since f is total, L_f being merely RE already makes f computable (dovetail the semi-decider over candidate outputs), so statement B is also true; A is the intended/official answer.

questions.q:
Let $L(R)$ be the language represented by regular expression $R$. Let $L(G)$ be the language generated by a context free grammar $G$. Let $L(M)$ be the language accepted by a Turing machine $M$. Which of the following decision problems are undecidable?

I. Given a regular expression $R$ and a string $w$, is $w \in L(R)$?

II. Given a context-free grammar $G$, is $L(G) = \emptyset$

III. Given a context-free grammar $G$, is $L(G) = \Sigma^*$ for some alphabet $\Sigma$?

IV. Given a Turing machine $M$ and a string $w$, is $w \in L(M)$?
questions.e:
**I is decidable.** Convert $R$ to an NFA (Thompson's construction) and simulate it on $w$, or convert it to a DFA and run that.

**II is decidable.** Mark the *generating* variables iteratively. A variable is generating if one of its productions has a body made only of terminals and already-marked variables. $L(G) = \emptyset$ iff the start symbol never gets marked.

**III is undecidable.** This is the universality problem for CFGs: does $G$ generate every string over its alphabet?
- It is undecidable, which is proved by reduction from PCP or by encoding the invalid computation histories of a TM as a CFL.
- Universality is decidable only for restricted classes, such as regular languages or deterministic CFLs.

**IV is undecidable.** This is the acceptance (membership) problem $A_{TM}$, which is undecidable by the standard diagonal argument. It is only semi-decidable, by simulating $M$ on $w$.

The undecidable problems are III and IV.

**Answer: (D)**

questions.q:
Consider the DFA $M$ and NFA $M_2$ as defined below. Let the language accepted by machine $M$ be $L$. What language machine $M_2$ accepts, if

- (i) $F2 = A$?
- (ii) $F2 = B$?
- (iii) $F2 = C$?
- (iv) $F2 = D$?

- $M = (Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_0, F)$
- $M_2 = (Q2, \Sigma, \delta_2, q_{00}, F2)$

Where,

$$
\begin{aligned}
Q2 &= (Q \times Q \times Q) \cup \{q_{00}\}\\
\delta_2(q_{00}, \epsilon) &= \{\langle q_0, q, q\rangle \mid q \in Q\}\\
\delta_2(\langle p, q, r\rangle, \sigma) &= \langle \delta(p, \sigma), \delta(q, \sigma), r\rangle \quad \text{for all } p, q, r \in Q \text{ and } \sigma \in \Sigma\\
A &= \{\langle p, q, r\rangle \mid p \in F;\ q, r \in Q\}\\
B &= \{\langle p, q, r\rangle \mid q \in F;\ p, r \in Q\}\\
C &= \{\langle p, q, r\rangle \mid p, q, r \in Q;\ \exists s \in \Sigma^*,\ \delta(p, s) \in F\}\\
D &= \{\langle p, q, r\rangle \mid p, q \in Q;\ r \in F\}
\end{aligned}
$$

a.text: (i) $L$; (ii) all suffixes of strings of $L$; (iii) all prefixes of strings of $L$; (iv) $\Sigma^*$ (or $\emptyset$ if $F=\emptyset$)

questions.e:
**Key idea.** After its single $\epsilon$-move, $M_2$ guesses a state $q \in Q$ and enters $\langle q_0, q, q\rangle$. From then on it runs three tracks in lock-step: track 1 simulates $M$ from $q_0$, track 2 simulates $M$ from the guessed state $q$, and track 3 never changes (it just remembers $q$). So after reading $w$ the NFA is in

$$\langle \hat\delta(q_0, w),\ \hat\delta(q, w),\ q\rangle, \qquad\text{hence}\qquad w \in L(M_2) \iff \exists q \in Q:\ \langle \hat\delta(q_0,w), \hat\delta(q,w), q\rangle \in F2 .$$

($q_{00} \notin F2$, so nothing is accepted without the $\epsilon$-move.)

**(i) $F2 = A$:** the condition is $\hat\delta(q_0, w) \in F$, independent of the guess. So $L(M_2) = L$.

**(ii) $F2 = B$:** the condition is $\hat\delta(q, w) \in F$ for some $q$. If $q = \hat\delta(q_0, x)$, this says exactly $xw \in L$. Hence $L(M_2) = \{w \mid \exists x \in \Sigma^*:\ xw \in L\}$, the set of all **suffixes** of strings in $L$. (This assumes every state of $M$ is reachable; in general it is $\{w \mid \exists q \in Q,\ \hat\delta(q, w) \in F\}$.)

**(iii) $F2 = C$:** the condition is that some final state can be reached from $p = \hat\delta(q_0, w)$, i.e. $\exists s:\ \hat\delta(q_0, ws) \in F \iff ws \in L$. So $L(M_2) = \{w \mid \exists s \in \Sigma^*:\ ws \in L\}$, the set of all **prefixes** of strings in $L$.

**(iv) $F2 = D$:** the condition is that the remembered guess satisfies $q \in F$, which does not depend on $w$ at all. If $F \neq \emptyset$, guess some $q \in F$; then every string (including $\epsilon$) is accepted, so $L(M_2) = \Sigma^*$. If $F = \emptyset$, then $L(M_2) = \emptyset$.

**Answer: (i) $L$; (ii) $\mathrm{Suffix}(L)$; (iii) $\mathrm{Prefix}(L)$; (iv) $\Sigma^*$ (or $\emptyset$ if $F = \emptyset$)**

questions.q: Let $L$ be the language of all binary strings in which the third symbol from the right is a $1$. Give a non-deterministic finite automaton that recognizes $L$. How many states does the minimized equivalent deterministic finite automaton have? Justify your answer briefly?

a.text: A 4-state NFA (shown below); the minimized DFA has 8 states

questions.e:
**NFA.** $L = (0+1)^*\,1\,(0+1)(0+1)$. The NFA loops in $q_0$ and nondeterministically guesses which $1$ is the third symbol from the right:

| State | 0 | 1 |
|---|---|---|
| $\to q_0$ | $\{q_0\}$ | $\{q_0, q_1\}$ |
| $q_1$ | $\{q_2\}$ | $\{q_2\}$ |
| $q_2$ | $\{q_3\}$ | $\{q_3\}$ |
| $q_3$ (final) | $\emptyset$ | $\emptyset$ |

**Minimized DFA: 8 states.** A DFA only needs to remember the last three symbols read. Use the states $b_1b_2b_3 \in \{0,1\}^3$, with the start state $000$ (shorter inputs act as if padded with leading 0's). The transitions are $b_1b_2b_3 \xrightarrow{c} b_2b_3c$, and the accepting states are those with $b_1 = 1$ ($100, 101, 110, 111$). That is 8 states.

**Why no DFA can use fewer (Myhill–Nerode).** Take two different 3-bit strings $x \neq y$. Let $i$ be the first position from the left where they differ, say $x_i = 1$ and $y_i = 0$. Appending $z = 0^{\,i-1}$ makes position $i$ the third symbol from the right, so $xz \in L$ but $yz \notin L$. So all 8 strings of length 3 are pairwise distinguishable, and each needs its own state.

In general, "the $n$-th symbol from the right is 1" needs $2^n$ DFA states, although an $(n+1)$-state NFA is enough.

**Answer: 4-state NFA as above; the minimized DFA has 8 states**

questions.q: Draw the state transition of a deterministic finite state automaton which accepts all strings from the alphabet $\{a, b\}$, such that no string has $3$ consecutive occurrences of the letter $b$.

a.text: A 4-state DFA counting trailing $b$'s ($q_0, q_1, q_2$ accepting; $q_3$ is a dead state)

questions.e:
**Key idea.** Remember how many $b$'s have just been read in a row (0, 1 or 2). A third consecutive $b$ sends the machine to a dead state.

| State | Meaning | a | b |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\to q_0$ (final) | no trailing $b$ | $q_0$ | $q_1$ |
| $q_1$ (final) | one trailing $b$ | $q_0$ | $q_2$ |
| $q_2$ (final) | two trailing $b$'s | $q_0$ | $q_3$ |
| $q_3$ (dead) | $bbb$ has occurred | $q_3$ | $q_3$ |

As a diagram: $q_0 \xrightarrow{b} q_1 \xrightarrow{b} q_2 \xrightarrow{b} q_3$. Every $a$ from $q_0$, $q_1$ or $q_2$ goes back to $q_0$, and $q_3$ loops on both $a$ and $b$. The final states are $q_0, q_1, q_2$. So $\epsilon$, $b$, $bb$ and $abbab$ are accepted, while $abbba$ is rejected.

**The DFA is minimal.** $q_3$ is the only non-final state. The final states are told apart by suffixes: $bb$ is accepted from $q_0$ but not from $q_1$, and $b$ is accepted from $q_0$ and $q_1$ but not from $q_2$.

An equivalent regular expression is $(a + ba + bba)^*(\epsilon + b + bb)$.

**Answer: 4-state DFA ($q_0, q_1, q_2$ accepting, $q_3$ dead)**

questions.q:
Given below are the transition diagrams for two finite state machines $M_1$ and $M_2$ recognizing languages $L_1$ and $L_2$ respectively.

Figure:

**$M_1$**: start state $A$; $A$ is a final state (double circle); $B$ is not final.

| State | 0 | 1 |
|---|---|---|
| $\to A$ (final) | $B$ | $B$ |
| $B$ | $A$ | $A$ |

**$M_2$**: start state $C$; $C$ and $D$ are final states (double circles); $E$ is not final.

| State | a | b |
|---|---|---|
| $\to C$ (final) | $C$ | $D$ |
| $D$ (final) | $E$ | $D$ |
| $E$ | $E$ | $E$ |

A. Display the transition diagram for a machine that recognizes $L_1.L_2$, obtained from transition diagrams for $M_1$ and $M_2$ by adding only $\varepsilon$ transitions and no new states.

B. Modify the transition diagram obtained in part (a) obtain a transition diagram for a machine that recognizes $(L_1.L_2)^*$ by adding only $\varepsilon$ transitions and no new states.

(Final states are enclosed in double circles).

a.text: (a) Add the $\varepsilon$-edge $A \to C$ (start $A$, final states $C, D$); (b) additionally add $\varepsilon$-edges $C \to A$ and $D \to A$

questions.e:
**What the machines accept.** $M_1$ alternates between $A$ and $B$ on every symbol and $A$ is final, so $L_1 = ((0+1)(0+1))^*$, the binary strings of even length. In $M_2$, the trap state $E$ is entered by reading $a$ after a $b$, and $C, D$ are final, so $L_2 = a^*b^*$. Note that $\varepsilon \in L_1$ and $\varepsilon \in L_2$.

**(a) $L_1.L_2$.** Add one $\varepsilon$-edge $A \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} C$, from the final state of $M_1$ to the start state of $M_2$. The start state is still $A$. $A$ is no longer final, and the final states are $C$ and $D$.

| State | 0 | 1 | a | b | $\varepsilon$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\to A$ | $B$ | $B$ | – | – | $C$ |
| $B$ | $A$ | $A$ | – | – | – |
| $C$ (final) | – | – | $C$ | $D$ | – |
| $D$ (final) | – | – | $E$ | $D$ | – |
| $E$ | – | – | $E$ | $E$ | – |

Why it works: an accepting path stays in $M_1$ until it takes the only bridge $A \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} C$. The part read before the bridge leads from $A$ back to $A$, so it is in $L_1$. The rest leads from $C$ to $C$ or $D$, so it is in $L_2$. (Keeping $A$ final would also be harmless here, because $\varepsilon \in L_2$ gives $L_1 \subseteq L_1L_2$.)

**(b) $(L_1.L_2)^*$.** Keep the machine from (a) and add $\varepsilon$-edges from its final states back to the start: $C \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} A$ and $D \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} A$. The start state is still $A$ and the final states are still $C$ and $D$. The $\varepsilon$-edges are now $A \to C$, $C \to A$ and $D \to A$.

Why it works: an accepting path is a sequence of rounds. In each round the machine goes from $A$ back to $A$ inside $M_1$ (reading a string of $L_1$), crosses $A \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} C$, and goes from $C$ to $C$ or $D$ inside $M_2$ (reading a string of $L_2$). Then it either stops in a final state or returns to $A$ by a new $\varepsilon$-edge. So exactly $(L_1L_2)^+$ is accepted. Since $\varepsilon \in L_1L_2$ (the path $A \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} C$ already accepts it), $(L_1L_2)^+ = (L_1L_2)^*$.

No new start state is needed. $A$ is never made final, so its incoming $0/1$ edges from $B$ cannot let any unwanted string be accepted.

**Answer: (a) add the $\varepsilon$-edge $A \to C$ (final states $C, D$); (b) also add the $\varepsilon$-edges $C \to A$ and $D \to A$**

questions.q:
Given that $L$ is a language accepted by a finite state machine, show that $L^P$ and $L^R$ are also accepted by some finite state machines, where

$L^P = \{s \mid ss' \in L \text{ some string } s'\}$

$L^R = \{s \mid s \text{ obtained by reversing some string in } L\}$

a.text: $L^P$: same DFA with every state that can reach a final state made final; $L^R$: reverse every edge, accept at the old start state, and add a new start state with $\epsilon$-edges to the old final states

questions.e:
Let $M = (Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_0, F)$ be a DFA with $L(M) = L$.

**$L^P$ (prefixes).** Keep $M$ unchanged except for its final states:

$$M^P = (Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_0, F'), \qquad F' = \{q \in Q \mid \exists s' \in \Sigma^*:\ \hat\delta(q, s') \in F\}.$$

$F'$ is the set of states from which some final state can be reached. It is computable by a graph search backwards from $F$, and it contains $F$. Correctness:

$$s \in L(M^P) \iff \hat\delta(q_0, s) \in F' \iff \exists s':\ \hat\delta(q_0, ss') \in F \iff \exists s':\ ss' \in L \iff s \in L^P .$$

So $M^P$ is a finite automaton accepting $L^P$.

**$L^R$ (reversal).** Build an NFA $N$ by running $M$ backwards:
- the states are $Q \cup \{q_s\}$, where $q_s$ is a new start state;
- add $q_s \xrightarrow{\epsilon} f$ for every $f \in F$;
- for every transition $\delta(p, a) = q$ of $M$, add the reversed transition $q \xrightarrow{a} p$;
- the only final state is $q_0$.

A path in $N$ reading $s = a_1a_2\cdots a_n$ goes $q_s \to f \to \cdots \to q_0$. Such a path exists exactly when $M$ has a path from $q_0$ reading $a_n\cdots a_2a_1$ that ends in $f \in F$, i.e. when $s^R \in L$. Hence $L(N) = L^R$. $N$ is a finite automaton (nondeterministic, with $\epsilon$-moves), and the subset construction gives an equivalent DFA. So $L^R$ is accepted by a finite state machine.

(If $F = \emptyset$ then $L = L^P = L^R = \emptyset$, and both constructions still work.)

**Answer: $L^P$ — same DFA with $F' = \{q : q \text{ can reach } F\}$; $L^R$ — reversed NFA starting from $F$ and accepting at $q_0$**

questions.q:
Construct DFA's for the following languages:

A. $L = \{w \mid w \in \{a, b\}^*,\ w \text{ has baab as a substring}\}$

B. $L = \{w \mid w \in \{a, b\}^*,\ w \text{ has an odd number of a's and an odd number of b's}\}$

a.text: (A) A 5-state DFA tracking progress through $baab$ (final trap state $q_4$); (B) a 4-state parity DFA whose only final state is (odd $a$, odd $b$)

questions.e:
**(A) Substring $baab$.** State $q_i$ means that the longest suffix of the input read so far which is also a prefix of $baab$ has length $i$. $q_4$ means $baab$ has already appeared; it is a final trap state.

| State | Matched so far | a | b |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\to q_0$ | – | $q_0$ | $q_1$ |
| $q_1$ | $b$ | $q_2$ | $q_1$ |
| $q_2$ | $ba$ | $q_3$ | $q_1$ |
| $q_3$ | $baa$ | $q_0$ | $q_4$ |
| $q_4$ (final) | $baab$ | $q_4$ | $q_4$ |

The fall-back moves work like this. From $q_1$ on $b$, "$bb$" still ends in $b$, so the machine stays in $q_1$. From $q_2$ on $b$, "$bab$" ends in $b$, so it goes to $q_1$. From $q_3$ on $a$, no suffix of "$baaa$" starts $baab$, so it goes to $q_0$.

The DFA is minimal: the shortest accepted continuation from $q_i$ has length $4 - i$, so all five states are distinguishable.

**(B) Odd number of $a$'s and odd number of $b$'s.** Each state records the two parities: $EE$ (start), $OE$, $EO$ and $OO$ (final), where the first letter is the parity of $a$'s and the second the parity of $b$'s. Reading $a$ flips the first parity and reading $b$ flips the second.

| State | a | b |
|---|---|---|
| $\to EE$ | $OE$ | $EO$ |
| $OE$ | $EE$ | $OO$ |
| $EO$ | $OO$ | $EE$ |
| $OO$ (final) | $EO$ | $OE$ |

For example, $ab$ and $babbaa$ are accepted, while $aab$ is rejected. This DFA is also minimal, since each state needs a different shortest accepted continuation: $\epsilon$, $a$, $b$ or $ab$.

**Answer: (A) 5-state DFA with final trap state $q_4$; (B) 4-state parity DFA with final state $OO$**

questions.q:
We require a four state automaton to recognize the regular expression $(a \mid b)^*abb$

A. Give an NFA for this purpose

B. Give a DFA for this purpose

a.text: NFA: $q_0$ loops on $a,b$ and $q_0 \xrightarrow{a} q_1 \xrightarrow{b} q_2 \xrightarrow{b} q_3$ (final); DFA: the 4-state machine tabulated below

questions.e:
**(A) NFA with 4 states.** $q_0$ loops on both symbols and guesses where the final $abb$ begins:

| State | a | b |
|---|---|---|
| $\to q_0$ | $\{q_0, q_1\}$ | $\{q_0\}$ |
| $q_1$ | $\emptyset$ | $\{q_2\}$ |
| $q_2$ | $\emptyset$ | $\{q_3\}$ |
| $q_3$ (final) | $\emptyset$ | $\emptyset$ |

**(B) DFA with 4 states.** The subset construction from $\{q_0\}$ reaches only $P_0 = \{q_0\}$, $P_1 = \{q_0, q_1\}$, $P_2 = \{q_0, q_2\}$ and $P_3 = \{q_0, q_3\}$. In words, $P_1$ means the input ends in $a$, $P_2$ that it ends in $ab$, and $P_3$ that it ends in $abb$.

| State | a | b |
|---|---|---|
| $\to P_0$ | $P_1$ | $P_0$ |
| $P_1$ | $P_1$ | $P_2$ |
| $P_2$ | $P_1$ | $P_3$ |
| $P_3$ (final) | $P_1$ | $P_0$ |

Check: $babb$ goes $P_0 \to P_0 \to P_1 \to P_2 \to P_3$ and is accepted. $abba$ ends in $P_1$ and is rejected.

The DFA is minimal. $P_3$ is the only final state, the suffix $b$ separates $P_2$ from $P_0$ and $P_1$, and the suffix $bb$ separates $P_1$ from $P_0$.

**Answer: NFA $q_0 \xrightarrow{a} q_1 \xrightarrow{b} q_2 \xrightarrow{b} q_3$ with an $a,b$ loop on $q_0$; DFA as tabulated with final state $P_3$**

questions.q:
The following diagram represents a finite state machine which takes as input a binary number from the least significant bit.

Figure (Mealy machine; edge labels are input/output; start state $Q_0$):

- $Q_0 \xrightarrow{0/0} Q_0$ (self-loop)
- $Q_0 \xrightarrow{1/1} Q_1$
- $Q_1 \xrightarrow{0/1} Q_1$ (self-loop)
- $Q_1 \xrightarrow{1/0} Q_1$ (self-loop)

Which of the following is TRUE?
o: It computes $1$'s complement of the input number
It computes $2$'s complement of the input number
questions.e:
**Key idea.** In $Q_0$ the bits are copied unchanged ($0/0$) up to the first $1$. That $1$ is also copied ($1/1$) and moves the machine to $Q_1$. In $Q_1$ every later bit is inverted ($0/1$, $1/0$). Copying from the LSB up to and including the first $1$, then complementing everything after it, is exactly the shortcut for the 2's complement.

**Example:** input $0110$ (six) is fed LSB first as $0, 1, 1, 0$. The outputs are $0$ (copy), $1$ (copy, go to $Q_1$), $0$ (inverted), $1$ (inverted). Read MSB first, the output is $1010$, and $1010 = 16 - 6$ is the 4-bit 2's complement of $0110$.

The other options would give: 1's complement $1001$, increment $0111$, decrement $0101$. None of these matches the machine's output.

Edge case: an all-zero input stays in $Q_0$ and outputs all zeros. That is also correct, since the 2's complement of 0 is 0.

**Answer: (B)**

questions.q:
Let $\delta$ denote the transition function and $\hat{\delta}$ denote the extended transition function of the $\epsilon$-NFA whose transition table is given below:

| $\delta$ | $\epsilon$ | $a$ | $b$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\to q_0$ | $\{q_2\}$ | $\{q_1\}$ | $\{q_0\}$ |
| $q_1$ | $\{q_2\}$ | $\{q_2\}$ | $\{q_3\}$ |
| $q_2$ | $\{q_0\}$ | $\emptyset$ | $\emptyset$ |
| $q_3$ | $\emptyset$ | $\emptyset$ | $\{q_2\}$ |

Then $\hat{\delta}(q_2, aba)$ is
questions.e:
**Key idea.** For an $\epsilon$-NFA, $\hat\delta(q, w)$ starts from the $\epsilon$-closure of $q$. After each input symbol, take all moves on that symbol and then the $\epsilon$-closure of the result.

**$\epsilon$-closures.** The $\epsilon$-edges are $q_0 \to q_2$, $q_1 \to q_2$ and $q_2 \to q_0$, so
- $E(q_0) = \{q_0, q_2\}$
- $E(q_1) = \{q_0, q_1, q_2\}$
- $E(q_2) = \{q_0, q_2\}$
- $E(q_3) = \{q_3\}$

**Trace of $aba$ from $q_2$:**
1. Start: $E(q_2) = \{q_0, q_2\}$.
2. Read $a$: $\delta(q_0, a) \cup \delta(q_2, a) = \{q_1\}$. The closure is $\{q_0, q_1, q_2\}$.
3. Read $b$: $\delta(q_0, b) \cup \delta(q_1, b) \cup \delta(q_2, b) = \{q_0\} \cup \{q_3\} \cup \emptyset = \{q_0, q_3\}$. The closure is $\{q_0, q_2, q_3\}$.
4. Read $a$: $\delta(q_0, a) \cup \delta(q_2, a) \cup \delta(q_3, a) = \{q_1\}$. The closure is $\{q_0, q_1, q_2\}$.

So $\hat\delta(q_2, aba) = \{q_0, q_1, q_2\}$.

Why the others fail:
- (D) is the set reached after reading only $ab$.
- (B) would need $q_3$ to survive the last $a$, but $\delta(q_3, a) = \emptyset$.
- (A) is wrong: $q_0$ is in the set before the last $a$, and $\delta(q_0, a) = \{q_1\}$, so the result is non-empty.

**Answer: (C)**

questions.q:
Let $M = (K, \Sigma, \sigma, s, F)$ be a finite state automaton, where

$K = \{A, B\}$, $\Sigma = \{a, b\}$, $s = A$, $F = \{B\}$,
$\sigma(A, a) = A$, $\sigma(A, b) = B$, $\sigma(B, a) = B$ and $\sigma(B, b) = A$

A grammar to generate the language accepted by $M$ can be specified as $G = (V, \Sigma, R, S)$, where $V = K \cup \Sigma$, and $S = A$.

Which one of the following set of rules will make $L(G) = L(M)$?
o: $\{A \rightarrow aB,\ A \rightarrow bA,\ B \rightarrow bA,\ B \rightarrow aA,\ B \rightarrow \epsilon\}$
$\{A \rightarrow aA,\ A \rightarrow bB,\ B \rightarrow aB,\ B \rightarrow bA,\ B \rightarrow \epsilon\}$
$\{A \rightarrow bB,\ A \rightarrow aB,\ B \rightarrow aA,\ B \rightarrow bA,\ B \rightarrow \epsilon\}$
$\{A \rightarrow aA,\ A \rightarrow bA,\ B \rightarrow aB,\ B \rightarrow bA,\ A \rightarrow \epsilon\}$
questions.e:
**Key idea.** A DFA turns into a right-linear grammar as follows: each transition $\sigma(X, c) = Y$ gives the rule $X \to cY$, each final state $X$ gives $X \to \epsilon$, and the start state is the start symbol.

- $\sigma(A, a) = A \Rightarrow A \to aA$
- $\sigma(A, b) = B \Rightarrow A \to bB$
- $\sigma(B, a) = B \Rightarrow B \to aB$
- $\sigma(B, b) = A \Rightarrow B \to bA$
- $B \in F \Rightarrow B \to \epsilon$

This is exactly option (B). The language is the set of strings with an odd number of $b$'s.

Why the other options fail:
- (A) has $A \to aB$ and $B \to \epsilon$, so it generates $a$, which $M$ rejects (zero $b$'s).
- (C) also has $A \to aB$ and $B \to \epsilon$, so it generates $a$ as well.
- (D) has $A \to \epsilon$ even though $A$ is not final, and $B$ can never be reached from $A$. It generates every string, including $\epsilon$.

**Answer: (B)**

questions.q:
Consider the non-deterministic finite automaton (NFA) shown in the figure.

Figure (start state $X$; no accepting state marked):

| State | 0 | 1 |
|---|---|---|
| $\to X$ | $\{Y, Z\}$ | $\{X\}$ |
| $Y$ | $\{Y, Z\}$ | $\emptyset$ |
| $Z$ | $\{X\}$ | $\{Y, Z\}$ |

(Edges: $X \xrightarrow{1} X$, $X \xrightarrow{0} Y$, $X \xrightarrow{0} Z$, $Y \xrightarrow{0} Y$, $Y \xrightarrow{0} Z$, $Z \xrightarrow{0} X$, $Z \xrightarrow{1} Y$, $Z \xrightarrow{1} Z$.)

State $X$ is the starting state of the automaton. Let the language accepted by the NFA with $Y$ as the only accepting state be $L1$. Similarly, let the language accepted by the NFA with $Z$ as the only accepting state be $L2$. Which of the following statements about $L1$ and $L2$ is TRUE?
questions.e:
**Key idea.** Run the subset construction from $\{X\}$. If every reachable subset that contains $Y$ also contains $Z$, and the other way round, then making $Y$ or $Z$ the accepting state gives the same language.

| Subset | on 0 | on 1 |
|---|---|---|
| $\{X\}$ | $\{Y, Z\}$ | $\{X\}$ |
| $\{Y, Z\}$ | $\{Y, Z\} \cup \{X\} = \{X, Y, Z\}$ | $\emptyset \cup \{Y, Z\} = \{Y, Z\}$ |
| $\{X, Y, Z\}$ | $\{X, Y, Z\}$ | $\{X, Y, Z\}$ |

Only three subsets are reachable: $\{X\}$, $\{Y, Z\}$ and $\{X, Y, Z\}$. In each of them, $Y$ is present exactly when $Z$ is. So for every input string the NFA can end in $Y$ if and only if it can end in $Z$, which means $L1 = L2$. Both equal $1^*0(0+1)^*$, the strings containing at least one $0$.

Because the languages are equal, neither proper-subset option (B) nor (C) holds, and (D) is wrong.

**Answer: (A)**

questions.q:
Consider the regular grammar:

- $S \rightarrow Xa \mid Ya$
- $X \rightarrow Za$
- $Z \rightarrow Sa \mid \epsilon$
- $Y \rightarrow Wa$
- $W \rightarrow Sa$

where $S$ is the starting symbol, the set of terminals is $\{a\}$ and the set of non-terminals is $\{S, W, X, Y, Z\}$.

We wish to construct a deterministic finite automaton (DFA) to recognize the same language. What is the minimum number of states required for the DFA?
questions.e:
**Key idea.** Eliminate the non-terminals to find the language. It turns out to be a unary language with period 3.

- From $Z \to Sa \mid \epsilon$ and $X \to Za$: $X \Rightarrow Saa$ or $X \Rightarrow a$.
- From $W \to Sa$ and $Y \to Wa$: $Y \Rightarrow Saa$.
- Substituting into $S \to Xa \mid Ya$ gives $S \to Saaa \mid aa$. The $Y$ branch adds nothing new.

So $L = aa(aaa)^* = \{a^n \mid n \equiv 2 \pmod 3\} = \{a^2, a^5, a^8, \dots\}$.

**Minimum DFA:** a 3-state cycle that counts $n \bmod 3$: $q_0 \xrightarrow{a} q_1 \xrightarrow{a} q_2 \xrightarrow{a} q_0$, with start state $q_0$ and final state $q_2$. No dead state is needed. The three states are pairwise distinguishable, since the shortest accepted continuations from $q_0$, $q_1$ and $q_2$ are $aa$, $a$ and $\epsilon$. Two states are not enough, because they cannot track $n \bmod 3$.

**Answer: (B)**

questions.q:
In the automaton below, $s$ is the start state and $t$ is the only final state.

Figure (the start state is drawn as $S$; the third state is unlabelled and is called $q$ here):

| State | $a$ | $b$ |
|---|---|---|
| $\to s$ (start) | $q$ | $t$ |
| $t$ (final) | $t$ | $s$ |
| $q$ | $s$ | $q$ |

(Edges: $s \xrightarrow{b} t$, $t \xrightarrow{b} s$, $t \xrightarrow{a} t$ (self-loop), $s \xrightarrow{a} q$, $q \xrightarrow{a} s$, $q \xrightarrow{b} q$ (self-loop).)

Consider the strings $u = abbaba$, $v = bab$, and $w = aabb$. Which of the following statements is true?
o: The automaton accepts $u$ and $v$ but not $w$
The automaton accepts each of $u, v,$ and $w$
The automaton rejects each of $u, v,$ and $w$
The automaton accepts $u$ but rejects $v$ and $w$
questions.e:
**Key idea.** The automaton is deterministic, so trace each string from $s$ and check whether it ends in $t$.

- $u = abbaba$: $s \xrightarrow{a} q \xrightarrow{b} q \xrightarrow{b} q \xrightarrow{a} s \xrightarrow{b} t \xrightarrow{a} t$. It ends in $t$, so $u$ is **accepted**.
- $v = bab$: $s \xrightarrow{b} t \xrightarrow{a} t \xrightarrow{b} s$. It ends in $s$, so $v$ is **rejected**.
- $w = aabb$: $s \xrightarrow{a} q \xrightarrow{a} s \xrightarrow{b} t \xrightarrow{b} s$. It ends in $s$, so $w$ is **rejected**.

Only $u$ is accepted:
- (A) is wrong because $v$ is rejected.
- (B) is wrong because $v$ and $w$ are rejected.
- (C) is wrong because $u$ is accepted.

**Answer: (D)**

questions.q:
For a state machine with the following state diagram the expression for the next state $S^+$ in terms of the current state $S$ and the input variables $x$ and $y$ is

Figure (state diagram with two states, $S = 1$ and $S = 0$):

- In state $S = 1$: on $x = 1$ it stays in $S = 1$ (self-loop); on $x = 0$ it goes to $S = 0$.
- In state $S = 0$: on $y = 1$ it stays in $S = 0$ (self-loop); on $y = 0$ it goes to $S = 1$.
questions.e:
**Key idea.** Find the next state for each value of the current state, then combine the two cases with $S$ and $S'$ as selectors:
$$S^+ = S\cdot(\text{next state when } S=1) + S'\cdot(\text{next state when } S=0).$$

- **When $S = 1$:** only $x$ matters. $x = 1$ keeps the machine in state 1 and $x = 0$ moves it to state 0, so $S^+ = x$.
- **When $S = 0$:** only $y$ matters. $y = 1$ keeps it in state 0 and $y = 0$ moves it to state 1, so $S^+ = y'$.

Combining the two cases gives $S^+ = S\,x + S'\,y'$, which is option (A).

Why the others are wrong:
- (B) With $S = 0$, $x = 0$, $y = 0$ it gives $S^+ = 0$, but the machine should move to state 1.
- (C) $x\,y'$ ignores $S$. With $S = 1$, $x = 1$, $y = 1$ it gives $0$, but the machine stays in state 1.
- (D) $S'y + Sx'$ gives the complement of the correct next state in both states.

**Answer: (A)**

questions.q:
Consider the following DFA in which $S_0$ is the start state and $S_1, S_3$ are the final states.

Figure (transition table of the DFA):

| State | $x$ | $y$ |
|---|---|---|
| $\to S_0$ (start) | $S_1$ | $S_3$ |
| $S_1$ (final) | $S_0$ | $S_2$ |
| $S_2$ | $S_3$ | $S_1$ |
| $S_3$ (final) | $S_2$ | $S_0$ |

What language does this DFA recognize?
o: All strings of $x$ and $y$ which have either even number of $x$ and even number of $y$ or odd number of $x$ and odd number of $y$
All strings of $x$ and $y$ which have equal number of $x$ and $y$
All strings of $x$ and $y$ with either even number of $x$ and odd number of $y$ or odd number of $x$ and even number of $y$
questions.e:
**Key idea.** Each $x$ swaps $S_0 \leftrightarrow S_1$ and $S_2 \leftrightarrow S_3$. Each $y$ swaps $S_0 \leftrightarrow S_3$ and $S_1 \leftrightarrow S_2$. So every state records the parity of the number of $x$'s and the parity of the number of $y$'s read so far:

| State | number of $x$ | number of $y$ |
|---|---|---|
| $S_0$ (start) | even | even |
| $S_1$ (final) | odd | even |
| $S_2$ | odd | odd |
| $S_3$ (final) | even | odd |

All eight edges agree with this table. For example, $S_1 \xrightarrow{y} S_2$ changes (odd, even) to (odd, odd), and $S_3 \xrightarrow{x} S_2$ changes (even, odd) to (odd, odd).

The final states are $S_1$ (odd $x$, even $y$) and $S_3$ (even $x$, odd $y$). The DFA therefore accepts exactly the strings with an even number of $x$ and an odd number of $y$, or an odd number of $x$ and an even number of $y$. Equivalently, it accepts the strings of odd length.

Why the others fail:
- (A) is wrong because $\epsilon$ (and $xy$) is rejected.
- (B) describes the non-final states $S_0$ and $S_2$.
- (C) is wrong because $xy$ has equal counts but ends in the non-final state $S_2$.

**Answer: (D)**

questions.q:
Consider the following finite automata $P$ and $Q$ over the alphabet $\{a, b, c\}$. The start states are indicated by a double arrow and final states are indicated by a double circle. Let the languages recognized by them be denoted by $L(P)$ and $L(Q)$ respectively.

Figure (in both automata **every** state is drawn as a final state; "–" means there is no transition):

**(P)**, start state $p_0$:

| State | $a$ | $b$ | $c$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\to p_0$ | $p_1$ | $p_2$ | – |
| $p_1$ | $p_3$ | $p_2$ | – |
| $p_2$ | $p_1$ | $p_3$ | – |
| $p_3$ | – | – | $p_2$ |

**(Q)**, start state $q_0$:

| State | $a$ | $b$ | $c$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\to q_0$ | $q_2$ | $q_1$ | – |
| $q_1$ | $q_2$ | – | – |
| $q_2$ | $q_3$ | $q_1$ | – |
| $q_3$ | – | $q_2$ | $q_1$ |

The automation which recognizes the language $L(P) \cap L(Q)$ is :

(Each option is drawn with states $r_0$ (start), $r_1$, $r_2$, $r_3$, all of them final; the edges of each are listed below.)
o: $r_0 \xrightarrow{a} r_1$, $r_0 \xrightarrow{b} r_2$, $r_1 \xrightarrow{a} r_3$, $r_1 \xrightarrow{b} r_2$, $r_2 \xrightarrow{a} r_1$, $r_3 \xrightarrow{c} r_2$
$r_0 \xrightarrow{a} r_1$, $r_0 \xrightarrow{b} r_2$, $r_1 \xrightarrow{b} r_2$, $r_1 \xrightarrow{b} r_3$, $r_2 \xrightarrow{a} r_1$, $r_3 \xrightarrow{c} r_2$
$r_0 \xrightarrow{a} r_1$, $r_0 \xrightarrow{b} r_2$, $r_1 \xrightarrow{b} r_2$, $r_1 \xrightarrow{b} r_3$, $r_2 \xrightarrow{a} r_1$, $r_2 \xrightarrow{b} r_3$, $r_3 \xrightarrow{c} r_2$
$r_0 \xrightarrow{a} r_1$, $r_0 \xrightarrow{c} r_2$, $r_1 \xrightarrow{b} r_2$, $r_1 \xrightarrow{b} r_3$, $r_2 \xrightarrow{a} r_1$, $r_2 \xrightarrow{b} r_3$, $r_3 \xrightarrow{c} r_2$
questions.e:
**Key idea.** Use the product construction: run $P$ and $Q$ in lock-step starting from $(p_0, q_0)$. A string is in $L(P) \cap L(Q)$ iff both machines can read all of it. Every state of $P$ and of $Q$ is final, so every reachable pair is final. A pair has no move on a symbol if either component has none.

Reachable pairs:

| Pair | $a$ | $b$ | $c$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $r_0 = (p_0, q_0)$ | $(p_1, q_2) = r_1$ | $(p_2, q_1) = r_2$ | – |
| $r_1 = (p_1, q_2)$ | $(p_3, q_3) = r_3$ | $(p_2, q_1) = r_2$ | – |
| $r_2 = (p_2, q_1)$ | $(p_1, q_2) = r_1$ | – ($q_1$ has no $b$) | – |
| $r_3 = (p_3, q_3)$ | – | – ($p_3$ has no $b$) | $(p_2, q_1) = r_2$ |

The product therefore has four final states and exactly these edges: $r_0 \xrightarrow{a} r_1$, $r_0 \xrightarrow{b} r_2$, $r_1 \xrightarrow{a} r_3$, $r_1 \xrightarrow{b} r_2$, $r_2 \xrightarrow{a} r_1$, $r_3 \xrightarrow{c} r_2$. This is option (A).

Why the others fail:
- (B) has no $a$-edge out of $r_1$, so it rejects $aa$. But $aa$ is in both languages: $p_0 \to p_1 \to p_3$ and $q_0 \to q_2 \to q_3$.
- (C) accepts $bb$ via $r_0 \to r_2 \to r_3$. But $Q$ cannot read $bb$, because $q_0 \xrightarrow{b} q_1$ and $q_1$ has no $b$-move.
- (D) accepts $c$, but $p_0$ has no $c$-move.

**Answer: (A)**

questions.q:
Consider the regular expression $R = (a+b)^*(aa+bb)(a+b)^*$

Which of the following non-deterministic finite automata recognizes the language defined by the regular expression $R$? Edges labeled $\lambda$ denote transitions on the empty string.

(Each option is an NFA with states $S_0, S_1, S_2, S_3$ and start state $S_0$. Its final states and edges are listed below, and $S_i \xrightarrow{a,b} S_i$ denotes a self-loop on both $a$ and $b$. None of the four drawn automata actually contains a $\lambda$-edge.)
o: Final state $S_3$. Edges: $S_0 \xrightarrow{a,b} S_0$, $S_0 \xrightarrow{a} S_1$, $S_0 \xrightarrow{b} S_2$, $S_1 \xrightarrow{a} S_3$, $S_1 \xrightarrow{b} S_2$, $S_2 \xrightarrow{a} S_1$, $S_2 \xrightarrow{b} S_3$, $S_3 \xrightarrow{a,b} S_3$

Final state $S_3$. Edges: $S_0 \xrightarrow{a} S_1$, $S_0 \xrightarrow{b} S_2$, $S_1 \xrightarrow{a,b} S_1$, $S_1 \xrightarrow{a} S_3$, $S_1 \xrightarrow{a} S_2$, $S_2 \xrightarrow{b} S_1$, $S_2 \xrightarrow{a,b} S_2$, $S_2 \xrightarrow{b} S_3$

Final state $S_3$. Edges: $S_0 \xrightarrow{a} S_1$, $S_0 \xrightarrow{b} S_2$, $S_1 \xrightarrow{a,b} S_1$, $S_1 \xrightarrow{a} S_3$, $S_1 \xrightarrow{b} S_2$, $S_2 \xrightarrow{a} S_1$, $S_2 \xrightarrow{a,b} S_2$, $S_2 \xrightarrow{b} S_3$

Final states $S_1$ and $S_3$. Edges: $S_0 \xrightarrow{a} S_1$, $S_0 \xrightarrow{b} S_2$, $S_1 \xrightarrow{a,b} S_1$, $S_1 \xrightarrow{a} S_3$, $S_1 \xrightarrow{b} S_2$, $S_2 \xrightarrow{a} S_1$, $S_2 \xrightarrow{a,b} S_2$, $S_2 \xrightarrow{b} S_3$, $S_3 \xrightarrow{a,b} S_3$
questions.e:
**Key idea.** $L(R)$ is the set of strings that contain $aa$ or $bb$. A correct NFA must (1) skip an arbitrary prefix, (2) detect a doubled letter, and (3) then accept whatever follows.

**(A) is correct.**
- The self-loop on $S_0$ skips any prefix.
- $S_1$ is entered only on an $a$ (from $S_0$ or $S_2$), and $S_2$ only on a $b$ (from $S_0$ or $S_1$).
- $S_3$ is entered either by an $a$ from $S_1$, which means $aa$ was just read, or by a $b$ from $S_2$, which means $bb$ was just read. So every accepted string contains $aa$ or $bb$.
- Conversely, take a string containing $aa$ (or $bb$). Loop on $S_0$ up to that pair, follow $S_0 \xrightarrow{a} S_1 \xrightarrow{a} S_3$ (or $S_0 \xrightarrow{b} S_2 \xrightarrow{b} S_3$), and read the rest on the loop at $S_3$.

Why the others fail:
- (B) and (C) both let $S_1$ loop on $b$. So they accept $aba$ via $S_0 \xrightarrow{a} S_1 \xrightarrow{b} S_1 \xrightarrow{a} S_3$, even though $aba$ contains neither $aa$ nor $bb$. (C) also has no loop on $S_3$ and rejects $aab \in L(R)$.
- (D) makes $S_1$ final, so it accepts $a \notin L(R)$.

**Answer: (A)**

questions.q:
Consider the regular expression $R = (a+b)^*(aa+bb)(a+b)^*$

Which deterministic finite automaton accepts the language represented by the regular expression $R$?

(Each option is drawn with start state $S_0$; its final states and edges are listed below.)
o: Final states $S_3, S_4$. Edges: $S_0 \xrightarrow{a} S_1$, $S_0 \xrightarrow{b} S_2$, $S_1 \xrightarrow{a} S_3$, $S_1 \xrightarrow{b} S_2$, $S_2 \xrightarrow{a} S_1$, $S_2 \xrightarrow{b} S_4$, $S_3 \xrightarrow{a} S_3$, $S_3 \xrightarrow{b} S_4$, $S_4 \xrightarrow{a} S_3$, $S_4 \xrightarrow{b} S_4$

Final states $S_3, S_4$. Edges: $S_0 \xrightarrow{a} S_1$, $S_0 \xrightarrow{b} S_2$, $S_1 \xrightarrow{a} S_3$, $S_1 \xrightarrow{b} S_4$, $S_2 \xrightarrow{a} S_3$, $S_2 \xrightarrow{b} S_4$, $S_3 \xrightarrow{a} S_3$, $S_3 \xrightarrow{a} S_4$, $S_4 \xrightarrow{b} S_4$, $S_4 \xrightarrow{b} S_3$

Final state $S_3$. Edges: $S_0 \xrightarrow{a} S_1$, $S_0 \xrightarrow{b} S_2$, $S_1 \xrightarrow{a} S_3$, $S_1 \xrightarrow{b} S_0$, $S_2 \xrightarrow{a} S_0$, $S_2 \xrightarrow{b} S_3$, $S_3 \xrightarrow{a,b} S_3$

Final state $S_3$. Edges: $S_0 \xrightarrow{a} S_1$, $S_0 \xrightarrow{b} S_2$, $S_1 \xrightarrow{a} S_0$, $S_1 \xrightarrow{b} S_3$, $S_2 \xrightarrow{a} S_3$, $S_2 \xrightarrow{b} S_0$, $S_3 \xrightarrow{a,b} S_3$
questions.e:
**Key idea.** To recognise "contains $aa$ or $bb$", a DFA only needs to remember the last symbol until the first doubled letter appears. After that it must stay in accepting states no matter what follows.

**(A) does exactly this.**
- $S_1$ means "last symbol was $a$" and $S_2$ means "last symbol was $b$", with no doubled letter seen yet. From $S_1$, an $a$ completes $aa$ (go to $S_3$) and a $b$ goes to $S_2$. From $S_2$, a $b$ completes $bb$ (go to $S_4$) and an $a$ goes to $S_1$.
- $S_3$ and $S_4$ are both final, and they only lead to each other. So once $aa$ or $bb$ has occurred, the string stays accepted.
- Every state has exactly one move on $a$ and one on $b$, so (A) is a valid DFA. It is not minimal, since $S_3$ and $S_4$ could be merged.

Why the others fail:
- (B) accepts $ab \notin L(R)$ via $S_0 \xrightarrow{a} S_1 \xrightarrow{b} S_4$. It is not even deterministic: $S_3$ has two $a$-moves.
- (C) returns to $S_0$ after $ab$ and so forgets the last $b$. For $abb$ it goes $S_0 \to S_1 \to S_0 \to S_2$ and rejects, although $abb$ contains $bb$.
- (D) accepts $ab$ via $S_0 \xrightarrow{a} S_1 \xrightarrow{b} S_3$.

**Answer: (A)**

questions.q:
If the final states and non-final states in the DFA below are interchanged, then which of the following languages over the alphabet $\{a, b\}$ will be accepted by the new DFA?

Figure (the states are unlabelled in the figure; they are called $q_0, q_1, q_2$ here):

| State | $a$ | $b$ |
|---|---|---|
| $\to q_0$ (start) | $q_1$ | $q_0$ |
| $q_1$ | $q_1$ | $q_2$ |
| $q_2$ (final) | $q_1$ | $q_0$ |
o: Set of all strings that do not end with $ab$
Set of all strings that begin with either an $a$ or $a\,b$
Set of all strings that do not contain the substring $ab$,
The set described by the regular expression $b^*aa^*(ba)^*b^*$
questions.e:
**Key idea.** First find the language of the original DFA. Since the DFA is complete (every state has both an $a$-move and a $b$-move), interchanging final and non-final states yields exactly the complement of that language.

What the states mean:
- $q_1$ is entered on every $a$, so it means "the last symbol is $a$".
- $q_2$ is entered only by a $b$ from $q_1$, so it means "the last two symbols are $ab$".
- $q_0$ covers everything else: $\epsilon$, or a string that ends in $b$ but not in $ab$.

The only final state is $q_2$, so the original DFA accepts exactly the strings ending in $ab$. After the swap, the new DFA accepts all strings that do **not** end with $ab$ (including $\epsilon$, $a$, $b$ and $aba$).

Why the others fail:
- (B) The new DFA accepts $b$, which does not begin with $a$.
- (C) This set is too small: $aba$ contains $ab$ but is accepted, since it ends in $q_1$.
- (D) The expression generates $ab$ (as $b^0\,a\,a^0\,(ba)^0\,b^1$), but the new DFA rejects $ab$.

**Answer: (A)**

questions.q:
Consider the following two finite automata. $M_1$ accepts $L_1$ and $M_2$ accepts $L_2$.

Figure (the states are unlabelled in the figure; they are named here):

**$M_1$** (start state $A$, final state $C$):

| State | 0 | 1 |
|---|---|---|
| $\to A$ | $A$ | $B$ |
| $B$ | $A$ | $C$ |
| $C$ (final) | $C$ | $C$ |

**$M_2$** (start state $X$, final state $Z$; non-deterministic):

| State | 0 | 1 |
|---|---|---|
| $\to X$ | $\{X\}$ | $\{X, Y\}$ |
| $Y$ | $\emptyset$ | $\{Z\}$ |
| $Z$ (final) | $\{Z\}$ | $\{Z\}$ |

Which one of the following is TRUE?
questions.e:
**Key idea.** Identify the two languages first, then test each claim.

- **$M_1$:** In $A$, no $11$ has been seen and the last symbol is not $1$. In $B$, no $11$ has been seen and the last symbol is $1$. A second consecutive $1$ moves to $C$, which accepts and never leaves, while a $0$ from $B$ resets to $A$. So $L_1$ is the set of strings that contain $11$.
- **$M_2$:** It loops in $X$ on any symbol, guesses where $11$ starts ($X \xrightarrow{1} Y \xrightarrow{1} Z$), then loops in $Z$. So $L_2 = (0+1)^*\,11\,(0+1)^*$, which is again the set of strings containing $11$.

Hence $L_1 = L_2$. Checking the options:
- (A) $L_1 = L_2$ is **true**.
- (B) $L_1 \subset L_2$ is false if $\subset$ means proper subset, and true if it means $\subseteq$.
- (C) $L_1 \cap L_2^C = \emptyset$ is **true**, because $L_1 \subseteq L_2$.
- (D) $L_1 \cup L_2 \neq L_1$ is false, because $L_1 \cup L_2 = L_1$.

At least two options, (A) and (C), are correct, so this single-answer question has no unique answer. Marks were awarded to all.

**Answer: Marks to all ((A) and (C) are both true; (B) too if $\subset$ means $\subseteq$)**

questions.q: What is the type of the language $L$, where $L = \{a^n b^n \mid 0 < n < 327\text{-th prime number}\}$

a.text: Regular (Type 3), because $L$ is a finite language

questions.e:
**Key idea:** the upper bound on $n$ is a fixed constant. So $L$ contains only finitely many strings, and every finite language is regular.

The 327-th prime is a specific number ($2179$), so
$$L = \{ab,\ a^2b^2,\ \dots,\ a^{2178}b^{2178}\},$$
a set of $2178$ strings. A finite language is regular. Its regular expression is simply the union of its finitely many strings. Equivalently, a DFA can remember the whole input up to length $2\cdot 2178$ and move to a dead state beyond that. Hence $L$ is **regular (Chomsky Type 3)**, and therefore also context-free, context-sensitive and recursive.

Contrast this with the unbounded language $\{a^nb^n \mid n \ge 1\}$, which is context-free but not regular. Its pumping-lemma proof needs a string $a^pb^p$ with $p$ larger than the pumping length, and that is impossible here because $n$ is bounded. When the counts are bounded, matching the number of $a$'s and $b$'s needs only a finite amount of memory.

**Answer: $L$ is regular (Type 3), since it is finite.**

questions.q: Show that the Turing machines, which have a read only input tape and constant size work tape, recognize precisely the class of regular languages.

a.text: Such a TM has finitely many internal configurations, so it is a two-way DFA, and two-way DFAs accept exactly the regular languages.

questions.e:
Let $M$ have:
- a finite control $Q$;
- a read-only input tape holding $\vdash w \dashv$ (with endmarkers), whose head may move both ways;
- a work tape of exactly $k$ cells over an alphabet $\Gamma$, where $k$ does not depend on the input.

**1. Every regular language is recognised by such a machine.** Take a DFA $A=(P,\Sigma,\delta,p_0,F)$. Let $M$ move its input head one cell right per step, change state according to $\delta$, and never use the work tape. When it reaches $\dashv$, it accepts iff its state is in $F$. Then $L(M)=L(A)$.

**2. Every such machine accepts a regular language.**

*(a) Fold the work tape into the finite control.* At any moment the work tape is fully described by its contents ($|\Gamma|^k$ possibilities) and the position of its head ($k$ possibilities). Use the new state set
$$Q' = Q \times \Gamma^k \times \{1,\dots,k\},$$
which is finite, of size $|Q|\cdot|\Gamma|^k\cdot k$. A machine with states $Q'$ and only the read-only two-way input head simulates $M$ step by step. So $M$ is equivalent to a **two-way DFA** $D$ with state set $Q'$. We may assume $D$ accepts only by halting on $\dashv$: whenever it would accept, it first walks right to $\dashv$.

*(b) Two-way DFAs accept only regular languages (Shepherdson).* For a string $x$, define a function $T_x : Q' \cup \{\bullet\} \to Q' \cup \{\bot\}$:
- $T_x(\bullet)$ is the state in which $D$, started normally at the left end, first moves off the right end of $\vdash x$. It is $\bot$ if that never happens.
- For a state $p$, $T_x(p)$ is the state in which $D$ next moves off the right end of $\vdash x$, after entering the last cell of $\vdash x$ from the right in state $p$. It is $\bot$ if $D$ never comes out.

$D$ can never leave on the left, because of $\vdash$.

Suppose $T_x = T_y$, and let $z$ be any string. Compare the runs of $D$ on $\vdash xz\dashv$ and on $\vdash yz\dashv$:
- Both leave the prefix in the same state $T_x(\bullet) = T_y(\bullet)$.
- They then move identically inside $z$ until they re-enter the prefix, both in the same state $p$.
- They come out again in the same state $T_x(p) = T_y(p)$, and so on.
- If one gets stuck inside the prefix ($\bot$), so does the other.

Hence $xz \in L(D) \iff yz \in L(D)$, so $x$ and $y$ are Myhill–Nerode equivalent. There are at most $(|Q'|+1)^{|Q'|+1}$ different functions $T_x$. So the Myhill–Nerode relation of $L(D)$ has finite index, and $L(D)$ is regular.

**Conclusion.** A read-only input tape cannot be used as extra storage, and a work tape of constant size adds only finitely many configurations. Such a machine therefore has only finite memory. By parts 1 and 2, these machines recognise exactly the regular languages.

**Answer: Folding the constant-size work tape into the finite control turns the machine into a two-way DFA, and two-way DFAs accept exactly the regular languages.**

questions.q:
A. Given a set:
$$S = \{x \mid \text{there is an } x\text{-block of 5's in the decimal expansion of } \pi\}$$
(Note: $x$-block is a maximal block of $x$ successive 5's)

Which of the following statements is true with respect to $S$? No reason to be given for the answer.

i. $S$ is regular
ii. $S$ is recursively enumerable
iii. $S$ is not recursively enumerable
iv. $S$ is recursive

B. Given that a language $L_1$ is regular and that the language $L_1 \cup L_2$ is regular, is the language $L_2$ always regular? Prove your answer.

a.text: A: (ii) $S$ is recursively enumerable; B: No, e.g. $L_1=\Sigma^*$ and $L_2=\{a^nb^n\}$

questions.e:
**Part A.**
- ***(ii) holds.*** The digits of $\pi$ are computable: an algorithm can print the $n$-th digit for any $n$. To semi-decide whether $x \in S$, generate the digits one by one and track the runs of 5's. A run is known to be maximal once a non-5 digit follows it, and every run does end because $\pi$ is irrational. Accept as soon as a maximal run of exactly $x$ fives has been completed. This procedure halts exactly when $x \in S$, so $S$ is recursively enumerable. Hence (iii) is false.
- ***(i) and (iv) cannot be asserted.*** To reject an $x \notin S$, one would have to know that no maximal run of exactly $x$ fives occurs anywhere in the infinite expansion, and no method for that is known. If $\pi$ is normal (widely believed, but unproved), then every pattern $d\,5^x d'$ with $d, d' \neq 5$ occurs. In that case $S=\{1,2,3,\dots\}$, which is recursive and even regular. Since this is an open problem, (i) and (iv) are not known to be true.
- ***Why "maximal" matters.*** Suppose "$x$-block" meant "at least $x$ successive 5's". Then $S$ would be either all of $\mathbb{N}$ or $\{1,\dots,k\}$ for some $k$. Either way it would be recursive (indeed regular), even though we would not know which case holds. With exact, maximal blocks this argument no longer works.

So the statement that can be asserted with certainty is **(ii)**.

**Part B. No.** Let $\Sigma = \{a,b\}$, $L_1 = \Sigma^*$ (regular) and $L_2 = \{a^nb^n \mid n \ge 0\}$. Then $L_1 \cup L_2 = \Sigma^*$ is regular.

$L_2$ is not regular. Suppose it were, with pumping length $p$. Write $a^pb^p = uvw$ with $|uv| \le p$ and $|v| \ge 1$. Then $v = a^t$ with $t \ge 1$, and $uv^2w = a^{p+t}b^p \notin L_2$, a contradiction.

So "$L_1$ regular and $L_1 \cup L_2$ regular" does **not** force $L_2$ to be regular, because a large regular $L_1$ can absorb any $L_2$. The same holds for intersection: $L_1 = \emptyset$ makes $L_1 \cap L_2 = \emptyset$ regular for every $L_2$.

**Answer: A: (ii) only ($S$ is recursively enumerable). B: No; $L_1=\Sigma^*$, $L_2=\{a^nb^n\}$ is a counterexample.**
questions.note: Part A: only (ii) is provable; (i) and (iv) depend on open questions about π (both would hold if π were normal), so the expected answer is debatable. Part B overlaps es_jaAxrLzd3VUh890k, which asks the same thing with L1 ∩ L2 instead of L1 ∪ L2.
